items.title: Integrated targeted metabolomics and complementary [α- 15 N] glutamine tracing reveal glutamine metabolic remodeling associated with RA-ILD.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis-associated interstitial lung disease (RA-ILD) is a severe complication with limited therapeutic options, characterized by destructive joint lesions and pulmonary fibrosis involving excessive collagen deposition. Glutamine metabolism supplies precursors for collagen-related amino acid biosynthesis, which drives the fibrotic remodeling process, but its cross-organ redistribution and pathway-specific utilization remain difficult to resolve using conventional metabolomic readouts. An analytical strategy capable of integrating quantitative multi-matrix profiling with isotope-resolved nitrogen tracing is therefore needed to characterize alterations in glutamine-related amino acid metabolism associated with RA-ILD and its pharmacological modulation. We established a complementary analytical framework in which 3-trimethylsilyl-1-propanaminium chloride (TSPC) derivatization-assisted UPLC-QqQ-MS/MS targeted metabolomics and intestinal amino acid transporter profiling were applied to an RA-ILD rat model, while [α- 15 N] glutamine tracing was independently performed in a TGF-β1-induced fibrotic cell model to examine pathway-specific glutamine nitrogen utilization. The validated method enabled sensitive quantification of glutamine-related amino acids in serum, lung tissue, and cells. In RA-ILD rats, cross-matrix profiling revealed a compartment-dependent disturbance of glutamine-related amino acid distribution, characterized by pulmonary accumulation coupled with altered circulating availability. Clematis triterpenoid saponins (CTSs) partially normalized this metabolic imbalance and were associated with coordinated regulation of intestinal glutamine transporters. Stable-isotope tracing in a fibrotic cell model further showed preferential incorporation of glutamine-derived nitrogen into the serine-glycine axis, which was supported by increased expression of ATF4-associated serine-glycine biosynthetic enzymes in lung tissue. CTSs treatment attenuated the corresponding lung transcriptional alterations. Together, invivo multi-matrix metabolomics characterized systemic glutamine-related metabolic redistribution and its response to CTSs in RA-ILD, whereas complementary in vitro isotope tracing provided pathway-level evidence for preferential glutamine-derived nitrogen utilization through the serine-glycine axis under fibrotic stimulation. Such a complementary framework also provides a transferable analytical strategy for investigating cross-organ diseases and multi-level interventions of traditional Chinese medicines.

items.title: Ocular involvement in Takayasu arteritis - A case series from a tertiary eye center in South India.
items.abstract: To analyze the clinical profile of patients with Takayasu arteritis (TAK) from a South Indian patient population who presented to a tertiary referral eye center. Retrospective case series between 2016 and 2025. Of the 13 cases of TAK, 11 were females and 2 were males (female: male = 11:2). The mean age was 31.92 ± 7.04 years. Nine cases initially presented to an ophthalmologist. The most common presenting symptoms were eye pain (eight cases) and diminution of vision (seven cases), of whom two had sudden vision loss. Ocular involvement included ocular ischemia with retinal vessel spasm and constriction (three cases), Takayasu retinopathy (three cases), and central retinal artery occlusion (one case). Optic disc pallor, dilated conjunctival and episcleral vessels, scleritis, hypertensive retinopathy, and atypical Tolosa Hunt syndrome were other presentations. Presumed ocular tuberculosis in two cases led to an incidental diagnosis of TAK. Based on the imaging findings, six cases had type I TAK, five cases had type V TAK, and one case each had type IV and type IIa TAK. Treatment included systemic corticosteroids and conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (methotrexate and mycophenolate mofetil) and tocilizumab. Good visual outcome on early treatment was seen in our series. TAK is an important and underrecognized cause of ocular inflammation and ischemia in young patients. Our series highlights that ocular involvement can precede systemic diagnosis. Early diagnosis and treatment results in a good visual outcome.

items.title: Chemically profiled total saponins of Panax japonicus C.A. Meyer attenuate rheumatoid arthritis-associated bone erosion and modulate osteoclastogenesis-associated SRC/TRAF6/NF-κB signaling.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA)-associated bone erosion is largely driven by excessive osteoclast differentiation and activation. Total saponins of Panax japonicus C.A. Meyer (TSPJs), a ginseng-derived botanical fraction, show anti-inflammatory activity in RA-related settings, but their effects on osteoclast-mediated bone destruction remain unclear. Transcriptomic datasets from RA synovial tissues and RANKL-induced osteoclast differentiation were integrated to identify shared pathogenic signals. TSPJs were chemically profiled by HPLC and evaluated in collagen-induced arthritis mice and RANKL-stimulated RAW264.7 cells. Osteoclast formation and function were assessed by TRAP staining, F-actin ring analysis, gene expression, bone resorption assays, histopathology, radiography, and serological measurements. Network pharmacology, molecular docking, CETSA, immunofluorescence, Western blotting, and immunohistochemistry were used to explore candidate mechanisms. Integrated bioinformatics highlighted NF-κB-related signaling as a shared pathway linking RA and osteoclastogenesis. HPLC identified four representative saponins: araloside A, chikusetsusaponin IVa, ginsenoside Rg2, and ginsenoside Ro. In CIA mice, TSPJs reduced arthritis severity, improved joint pathology, lowered osteoclast-associated serum markers, and attenuated radiographic and histological bone erosion. In vitro, TSPJs inhibited RANKL-induced osteoclast differentiation, disrupted F-actin rings, downregulated osteoclast-related genes, and reduced bone resorption. The overall evidence was consistent with modulation of SRC/TRAF6/NF-κB signaling, while docking and CETSA supported SRC/NFATc1/FOS-related nodes as candidates for further validation. TSPJs attenuated RA-associated bone erosion and restrained osteoclastogenesis, supporting further evaluation of this Panax japonicus -derived saponin preparation.

items.title: The effects of foot massage and textured insoles on balance and plantar sensation in individuals with rheumatoid arthritis.
items.abstract: Foot involvement is common in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and contributes to impaired balance, altered plantar sensation, and functional limitations. Whether textured insoles provide additional benefits when combined with foot massage remains unclear. To investigate the additional effects of textured insoles combined with foot massage on balance, plantar sensation, and foot function in individuals with RA. Twenty-nine individuals with RA in remission were randomly assigned to a foot massage plus textured insoles ( n  = 15) or a foot massage alone ( n  = 14). Both groups received foot massage three times weekly for six weeks, while the intervention group additionally wore textured insoles. Assessments were performed at baseline (T0), after the 6-week massage program (T1), and 8 weeks later (T2), with textured insole use continuing between T1 and T2. The primary outcome was balance assessed using the modified Sensory Organization Test (mSOT). Secondary outcomes included other balance measures, plantar sensation, and the Foot Function Index (FFI). Modified intention-to-treat (mITT) and per-protocol (PP) analyses were performed. No consistent between-group differences were observed for the primary mSOT outcome, other balance measures, or plantar sensation. The intervention group showed greater improvements in the FFI disability (mITT: p  = .027; PP: p  = .034) and total FFI score (mITT: p  = .024; PP: p  = .011) at T2. No significant between-group differences were found for the FFI pain or activity limitation. Adding textured insoles to foot massage did not provide consistent additional benefits for balance or plantar sensation in individuals with RA in remission. Between-group differences favoring the textured insole group were observed in foot-related disability and overall foot function; however, these were secondary outcomes and should be considered exploratory. These findings require confirmation in larger, adequately powered, sham-controlled trials.

items.title: Real‑world assessment of the effectiveness and response profiles of biologic DMARDs in psoriatic arthritis: findings from an emulated multicentre clinical trial.
items.abstract: To evaluate 6-month effectiveness and long-term drug-retention rates of biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (bDMARDs) in psoriatic arthritis (PsA) using real-world data analysed within an emulated multicentre clinical trial framework. Secondary objectives included the characterisation of response profiles and the identification of possible predictors of clinical response across bDMARD classes. Between January 2022 and June 2025, consecutive patients with moderate-to-high PsA disease activity initiating a bDMARD were prospectively enrolled in a multicentre Gruppo Italiano di Ricerca in Reumatologia Clinica e Sperimentale study. Real-world data were analysed within a target trial emulation framework comparing tumour necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors, interleukin (IL)-17 inhibitors, and IL-23-pathway inhibitors. Propensity score weighting was used to improve comparability in measured baseline characteristics across treatment groups. Effectiveness was assessed through longitudinal changes in the Disease Activity Index for Psoriatic Arthritis (DAPSA) over 6 months. Subsequent long-term drug retention was evaluated using a 6-month landmark analysis restricted to patients who remained on the index bDMARD at month 6. Potential clinical factors associated with treatment response and discontinuation were also explored. Overall, 990 patients were included: 342 initiated TNF inhibitors, 313 IL-17 inhibitors, and 335 IL-23-pathway inhibitors. DAPSA decreased significantly over 6 months in all 3 treatment groups, with no statistically significant between-class differences in adjusted longitudinal trajectories. Among patients who remained on the index bDMARD through month 6, the adjusted analyses did not identify statistically significant between-class differences in subsequent long-term drug retention. Shorter disease duration was associated with more favourable outcomes in selected exploratory analyses, whereas associations with previous bDMARD exposure were inconsistent. Additional class-specific associations were identified but should be considered exploratory and hypothesis-generating. Adverse-event-related discontinuations documented in routine clinical records were described; however, the study was not designed to support formal comparative safety conclusions. In this real-world emulated multicentre clinical trial, bDMARDs showed comparable overall trajectories of short-term effectiveness and long-term treatment persistence in PsA. The identification of partially distinct response patterns may support a more individualised approach to bDMARD selection.

items.title: A Paeoniae Radix Alba Polysaccharide Fraction BP-1 Restores Intestinal Barrier Function and Gut Microbiota-Metabolic Homeostasis in Collagen-Induced Arthritis Rats.
items.abstract: Paeoniae Radix Alba (PRA) polysaccharides are promising food-derived bioactives, yet their gut-mediated effects on rheumatoid arthritis (RA) remain unclear. Here, BP-1 was purified, structurally characterized, and evaluated in collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) rats and lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-injured Caco-2 cells. BP-1 was a 14.124 kDa neutral polysaccharide mainly composed of glucose and mannose. NMR analysis identified →4)-α-D-Glcp-(1→, →4,6)-α-D-Glcp-(1→, α-T-D-Glcp-(1→, →4,6)-β-D-Manp-(1→, and α-T-D-Galp-(1→ residues. BP-1 alleviated arthritis severity, joint pathology, systemic inflammation, and colonic injury, while improving intestinal barrier integrity in vivo and in vitro. These effects were potentially associated with suppression of TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB signaling, restoration of immune homeostasis, and modulation of gut microbiota and fecal metabolites. These findings support BP-1 as a potential functional food ingredient for inflammation-associated intestinal and immune disorders.

items.title: The development and validation of a new diagnostic sonographic enthesitis score for psoriatic arthritis: Diagnostic Ultrasound Enthesitis Tool (DUET).
items.abstract: The Diagnostic Ultrasound Enthesitis Tool (DUET) study aimed to develop and validate a new sonographic scoring system for enthesitis to aid PsA diagnosis. We prospectively enrolled patients with early PsA, psoriasis without arthritis (PsO), and non-inflammatory musculoskeletal symptoms as controls (CTL) from 17 centers. A standardized ultrasound assessment of 16 entheseal sites was performed and images were centrally scored by three blinded readers for inflammatory and structural entheseal lesions. Using a stepwise approach with logistic regression models stratified by age, we identified optimal lesion combinations, weightings, and entheseal sites for distinguishing PsA from CTL. Age-specific cut-off points were selected to maintain specificity above 70%. Performance was assessed in a validation cohort of PsA and CTL. We included 213 PsA, 100 PsO, and 106 CTL in the discovery cohort. The final DUET score combined weighted inflammatory (hypoechogenicity + thickening + Doppler grade x 2) and structural (enthesophyte grade + erosion x 3) scores at three entheseal sites: Achilles, proximal patellar tendon insertion, and triceps. Age stratification (≤55 vs. >55 years) improved discriminative performance. In the discovery cohort, DUET achieved an AUC of 0.65, with specificity of 73-74% and sensitivity of 47-49%. In an external validation cohort (101 PsA, 69 CTL), specificity improved to 74-100% with similar sensitivity (49-52%). Sensitivity increased up to 63% in patients with tender entheses. DUET is a novel, externally validated sonographic enthesitis score that could support the diagnostic assessment of patients with early PsA, particularly in individuals with tender entheses.

items.title: Risk stratification of severe infections after remission induction therapy in idiopathic inflammatory myopathy: a multicentre myko study.
items.abstract: To identify baseline predictors and develop a clinical risk stratification model for severe infections (SI) in patients with idiopathic inflammatory myopathy (IIM) after remission induction therapy. We enrolled patients diagnosed with IIM between 1991 and 2024 from three Japanese centres participating in the multicentre Idiopathic Inflammatory Myopathy and Anti-synthetase Syndrome (MYKO) cohort. SI was defined as an infection requiring intravenous antibiotics or hospitalisation. We explored the risk factors for predicting SI in patients with IIM by comparing the initial demographic, clinical, laboratory, and treatments between the SI and non-SI groups. Among 349 patients with IIM, 14.6% of patients developed SIs after remission induction therapy over a median follow-up of 4.7 years. Patients who developed SI　 exhibited significantly lower baseline albumin levels, and significantly higher baseline C-reactive protein (CRP), lactate dehydrogenase, and surfactant protein (SP-D) levels than those without SI. Multivariate logistic regression analysis demonstrated that elevated CRP and SP-D levels were independently associated with SI. Serum CRP levels remained significantly higher in the SI group than in the non-SI group over the two-year period after immunosuppressive therapy, and the serum SP-D levels tended to be higher in the SI group. The 10-year SI rate was significantly different among patients with IIM stratified by the number of risk factors, defined as CRP ≥ 0.8 mg/dL and SP-D ≥ 96.2 ng/mL. This model, which consists of CRP ≥ 0.8 mg/dL, SP-D ≥ 96.2 ng/mL, is useful for clinical risk stratification of SI after remission induction therapy in IIM.

items.title: Longitudinal ultrasound assesment of skeletal muscle ın systemic sclerosis: association with disease activity and severity.
items.abstract: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is an autoimmune fibroinflammatory disease that may predispose to the development of muscle loss through chronic inflammation and functional limitation. Longitudinal assessment using ultrasound provides insights into muscle loss and its association with disease activity and severity. This study sought to evaluate early muscle loss using ultrasound in SSc patients and investigate their relationship with disease activity and severity. A longitudinal study was conducted in 52 SSc patients, with muscle thickness at various sites, including biceps brachii, triceps brachii, medial gastrocnemius, and the rectus femoris measured at 0, 6, and 12. months using ultrasound. Associations with disease activity, Medsger's Severity Score and modified Rodnan skin score (mRSS) were analyzed. The diagnostic value of changes in muscle thickness for determining disease activity was assessed using ROC curve analysis. A significant inverse correlation was identified between the change in gastrocnemius muscle thickness and disease activity over the initial 6-month period (r=-0.36, p = 0.026). A significant relationship was found between the difference in mRSS and the difference in biceps brachii muscle thickness between baseline and 6 months (r=-0.33, p < 0.05). Decreasing muscle thickness paralleled increasing severity scores. ROC analysis for gastrocnemius muscle indicated moderate discriminative performance for detecting clinically relevant muscle changes. Longitudinal ultrasound assessment effectively reflects progressive reduction in muscle thickness in SSc, correlating with disease activity and severity. These findings highlight ultrasound as a practical, non-invasive tool for early detection and monitoring, potentially capturing subclinical changes, specifically a decrease in muscle thickness, in SSc.

items.title: Conductive and sensorineural hearing impairment in juvenile idiopathic arthritis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.abstract: To determine the prevalence of ossicular stiffness and cochlear dysfunction in patients with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) compared with healthy controls. We searched PubMed (1966-27 December 2025), Embase (1947-27 December 2025), and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (1996-27 December 2025). Studies of patients diagnosed with JIA who underwent audiological examinations (cochlear and middle ear function) were selected for the review. Random-effects models were used to calculate pooled relative risks (RR) and standardized mean differences (SMD). Seven studies (237 patients with JIA; 132 healthy controls) were included; six were judged high methodological quality (Newcastle-Ottawa score ≥ 8). Children with JIA exhibited a markedly higher prevalence of type As tympanograms (RR = 13.93, 95% CI 5.83-33.27) and elevated pure-tone hearing thresholds, with the largest effect observed at the extended high frequency of 16 kHz (SMD = 1.52, 95% CI 1.04-1.99). Pooled otoacoustic emission amplitudes trended lower in JIA but did not reach statistical significance (SMD = -1.72, 95% CI - 8.77 to 5.33; I² = 96%), although the single study reporting DPOAE suggested a marked reduction. JIA is associated with a quantifiable dual-compartment audiological burden-a markedly elevated risk of mechanical middle-ear stiffness and a frequency-dependent sensorineural deficit most pronounced beyond the conventional audiometric range. Tympanometry and extended high-frequency audiometry may provide complementary information for detecting subclinical auditory involvement in JIA. The potential role of OAEs, including DPOAE, requires confirmation in larger prospective studies.

items.title: Contextual laboratory interpretation of anti-topoisomerase I positivity in systemic sclerosis: a de-duplicated real-world analysis.
items.abstract: To assess how routinely available serological findings contextualize anti-topoisomerase I positivity in systemic sclerosis (SSc). We reanalyzed a single-center 2023 cohort using the earliest qualifying record per patient and strict recorded inpatient SSc diagnoses. Logistic models evaluated antibody signal intensity and antinuclear antibody (ANA) status, titer, and pattern. An available chemiluminescence immunoassay (CLIA) subset provided orthogonal analytical context. Among 669 patients with line-immunoassay (LIA) grayscale values >25 for anti-topoisomerase I, 440 were ANA-positive and 229 ANA-negative; SSc was recorded in 69/440 (15.7 %) and 2/229 (0.9 %), respectively. LIA intensity (per 10 units; OR 1.43, 95 % CI 1.30-1.58) and ANA positivity (OR 10.57, 95 % CI 2.51-44.57) were independently associated with recorded SSc. Adding ANA status increased AUC from 0.815 to 0.847 (p=0.011). Within ANA-positive patients, LIA intensity, ANA titer ≥1:160, and non-AC-29 pattern were independently informative; adding pattern increased AUC from 0.817 to 0.862 (p=0.011). In 268 CLIA observations, confirmation increased with LIA intensity; unadjusted rates were 74/122 (60.7 %) for ANA-positive and 61/146 (41.8 %) for ANA-negative observations (p=0.002). ANA status, LIA intensity, titer, and AC-29 provide complementary laboratory context for interpreting anti-topoisomerase I positivity.

items.title: IgG78-Engineered Macrophage Membrane Biomimetic Nanoparticles for Synergistic Targeted Photothermal-Chemotherapy of Rheumatoid Arthritis.
items.abstract: Clinical management of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) primarily involves non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), glucocorticoids, disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs), and biological agents or gene therapy; however, these treatments have notable limitations. DMARDs, particularly methotrexate (MTX), continue to be the cornerstone of first-line therapy, despite systemic side effects that restrict long-term application and heighten the treatment burden. This study identified elevated levels of CD248 in synovial fibroblasts (RA-FLS) from RA patients, which correlated with increased proliferation and migration. To improve the joint targeting of MTX, a biomimetic nanoplatform was developed using macrophage membrane coating. The anti-CD248 antibody (IgG78) was conjugated to the macrophage membrane surface and incorporated onto mesoporous polydopamine (MPDA) nanoparticles, resulting in active-targeting membrane-coated nanoparticles (MNPs). Experimental results demonstrated that MNPs exhibit exceptional specificity and affinity for RA-FLS. The MTX-loaded MPDA/MTX@M-IgG78 nanosystem showed pronounced therapeutic effects against RA. The high photothermal conversion efficiency of MPDA facilitated controlled MTX release under near-infrared laser irradiation, synergistically enhancing anti-RA efficacy. In conclusion, this innovative biomimetic approach enables targeted MTX delivery to the joints, improving therapeutic effectiveness while minimizing systemic side effects, thereby providing novel strategies for precise RA treatment.

items.title: Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis With Bilateral Blindness in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus: A Case Report.
items.abstract: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) is an uncommon but potentially life-threatening neurological complication of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) that requires prompt recognition and treatment. We report the case of an 18-year-old Bangladeshi woman with established SLE who presented with a 10-day history of severe headache followed by rapidly progressive bilateral proptosis and sudden, painless bilateral visual loss. Neurological examination revealed complete bilateral visual loss, bilateral ptosis, restricted extraocular movements and multiple cranial nerve deficits. She had active SLE with severe thrombocytopaenia and haematological involvement. Brain magnetic resonance imaging and magnetic resonance venography demonstrated extensive thrombosis involving the superior sagittal, bilateral transverse and sigmoid and cavernous sinuses. Antiphospholipid antibody testing, including lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibodies and Anti-β2-glycoprotein I antibodies, was negative. The patient received therapeutic anticoagulation, high-dose corticosteroids and immunosuppressive therapy with rituximab, followed by haematological and neurological improvement and subsequent recanalisation of the thrombosed dural venous sinuses. However, bilateral visual loss persisted, with optic disc pallor and optic atrophy. Optical coherence tomography, visual evoked potential testing, dedicated orbital imaging and formal neuro-ophthalmological assessment were not performed; therefore, the precise mechanism of visual loss could not be definitively established. Nevertheless, ischaemic optic neuropathy was considered the most likely mechanism given the clinical presentation and extensive CVST. This case highlights that extensive CVST may occur in active SLE despite negative antiphospholipid antibody testing. It underscores the importance of early neuroimaging, timely anticoagulation and appropriate immunosuppressive therapy to minimise the risk of persistent neurological and visual sequelae.

items.title: Diffuse large B cell lymphoma in rheumatoid arthritis express polyreactive and autoreactive BCRs binding protein modifications.
items.abstract: An important risk factor for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) development in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is high cumulated disease activity. B cell intrinsic factors and autoimmune processes may contribute, and we hypothesize that BCR autoreactivity may drive lymphomagenesis and/or lymphoma cell survival. RA is primarily associated with anti-citrullinated protein autoantibodies but patients can also have other anti-modified protein autoantibodies, e.g. towards malondialdehyde acetaldehyde (MDA/MAA) adducts which correlate with disease activity and inflammation. Here, we investigated DLBCL properties from RA patients with concurrent lymphoma by B-cell receptor (BCR) next generation sequencing and re-expression. In total 22 RA-DLBCL patients were included from the Swedish AUTO-LYMPHOMA cohort. Tumour DNA was extracted from fixed tissues and full length VH/VL fragments were amplified by multiplex PCR and sequenced using Illumina. Computational analysis assessed clonal variations. Dominating sequences were synthesized and expressed as recombinant monoclonal antibodies for antigen binding analysis. Complete VH/VL lymphoma tissue sequences were generated from nine RA-DLBCL patients. Clonotype diversity within the tumour was generally low and the dominant paired heavy and light chain BCR sequences were obtained for six patients. For three patients, amino acid variations in the DLBCL clonotype indicated intra-clonal evolution. Two of six patients had tumour BCRs with few VH and VL somatic hypermutations (≤ 5 mismatches) while three had high mutations (> 15 VH or VL mismatches). No bias in VH/VL usage was detected. Six lymphoma BCRs from five patients were expressed as recombinant monoclonal antibodies and their binding to autoantigens was assessed by ELISA and a solid-phase microarray (> 400 antigens). All patient-derived lymphoma BCRs were CCP2 negative, but five bound MDA/MAA-protein. Three of these displayed polyreactive binding by in-house assays of which two further displayed strikingly broad polyreactivity on the antigen array. Importantly, for one patient, the lymphoma BCR had high specificity to MDA/MAA-protein, and another patient DLBCL-BCR had binding only to methylated protein. The data suggest a possible link between polyreactivity and anti-MDA/MAA autoreactivity in RA-DLBCL lymphomagenesis. We hypothesize that high inflammation burden could increase antigen load which may trigger polyreactive and modified-protein B cell responses and/or maintain lymphoma cell survival.

items.title: Towards rheumatoid arthritis prevention: integrating mechanistic and omics insights.
items.abstract: Seropositive rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune disease whose course typically begins before joint involvement, during a period termed pre-RA, which is initially characterized by the presence of autoantibodies, including anti-citrullinated protein antibodies and rheumatoid factors. The ability to identify autoantibody-positive individuals who are at an increased risk of developing clinical RA has catalysed efforts to define the immune mechanisms underlying the initial break in self-tolerance and the subsequent transition to clinically apparent disease. Although not mutually exclusive, these investigations have broadly followed two complementary approaches: hypothesis-testing studies and agnostic multi-omics analysis. Hypothesis-testing studies have identified site-specific and isotype-specific patterns of mucosal anti-citrullinated protein antibodies and rheumatoid factor production, together with inflammation and/or dysbiosis associated with systemic autoimmunity, supporting a 'mucosal origins hypothesis'. Cross-sectional and longitudinal multi-omics studies have demonstrated epitope spreading, pro-inflammatory biomarkers and dysregulated peripheral blood immune-cell populations with autoimmune characteristics. Epidemiological studies have further implicated certain environmental exposures in RA development. Collectively, these observations suggest that integrating molecular, cellular and environmental data through emerging data science and artificial intelligence approaches could help to identify pathogenic mechanisms underlying RA development and inform future prevention strategies.

items.title: High-resolution computed tomography imaging of pulmonary changes and relation with disease activity in rheumatoid arthritis.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic systemic inflammatory disease with a wide spectrum of pulmonary manifestations, some of which may remain clinically occult. High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) is an important imaging modality for detecting and characterizing these abnormalities. This study aimed to evaluate the spectrum of thoracic HRCT abnormalities in patients with RA and examine their association with disease activity and inflammatory markers. A prospective, analytical, hospital-based cross-sectional study was conducted from January 2021 to January 2022, including 63 adults with RA fulfilling the 2010 American College of Rheumatology/European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology classification criteria. Clinical characteristics, disease activity assessed using the Disease Activity Score 28-erythrocyte sedimentation rate (DAS28-ESR), inflammatory markers, and thoracic HRCT findings were recorded and analyzed. Of the 63 patients, 45 (71.4%) were women, and the mean age was 45.3±13.4 years. HRCT abnormalities were detected in 36 (57.1%) patients, with usual interstitial pneumonia-pattern interstitial lung disease (22.2%) and ground-glass opacities (19.0%) being the most frequent findings. Patients with abnormal HRCT findings had significantly higher DAS28-ESR scores, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rates, and longer disease duration compared with those with normal HRCT findings (all p<0.001). C-reactive protein positivity (p<0.001) and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody positivity (p=0.012) were also significantly associated with HRCT abnormalities, whereas age and sex showed no significant associations. Pulmonary abnormalities detected by HRCT were common in patients with RA and were associated with greater disease activity, systemic inflammation, and longer disease duration. These findings highlight the importance of respiratory assessment in patients with RA, particularly those with active disease.

items.title: Case Report: Monotypic IgG1-λ fibrillary glomerulonephritis associated with rheumatoid arthritis.
items.abstract: Fibrillary glomerulonephritis (FGN) is a rare glomerular disease characterized by non-amyloid fibrillary deposits and is identified in fewer than 1% of native kidney biopsies. Most cases demonstrate polytypic immunoglobulin G deposition, whereas confirmed monotypic FGN is exceptionally uncommon and may raise concern for an underlying monoclonal gammopathy. A 72-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis presented with nephrotic-range proteinuria (4.6 g/24 h), microscopic hematuria, hypoalbuminemia, lower-extremity edema, and mildly impaired kidney function. Kidney biopsy demonstrated mesangial expansion and glomerular deposits staining for IgG, C3, and lambda light chain. The deposits were Congo red negative and showed strong, diffuse glomerular DNAJB9 positivity. Electron microscopy revealed randomly oriented, non-branching fibrils measuring approximately 20 nm, accompanied by podocyte foot-process effacement. Isolated IgG1 staining and lambda restriction, confirmed by immunofluorescence performed on pronase-digested paraffin-embedded tissue, supported a true monotypic IgG1-lambda phenotype. Serum immunofixation and serum free light-chain testing did not demonstrate a monoclonal protein, and no underlying hematological malignancy, other malignancy, or infection was identified. The patient received rituximab. At 14 months, proteinuria had decreased to approximately 1.0 g/24 h and serum albumin had increased from 30 to 38 g/L. Confirmed monotypic FGN is exceptionally rare and requires integration of routine immunofluorescence, IgG-subclass assessment, paraffin-embedded immunofluorescence, DNAJB9 immunohistochemistry, and electron microscopy. Light-chain restriction alone is insufficient to establish a truly monotypic process, and monotypic deposits warrant careful evaluation for an underlying clonal disorder. This case documents DNAJB9-positive monotypic IgG1-lambda FGN occurring in the setting of rheumatoid arthritis without demonstrable monoclonal gammopathy.

items.title: Incidence and prevalence of hidradenitis suppurativa across spondyloarthritis-related diseases: cohort study using electronic health records.
items.abstract: To describe the recorded prevalence and incidence of HS across pathologically related diseases within the spondyloarthritis (SpA) family, namely psoriatic arthritis (PsA), psoriasis, axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA), uveitis, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, and, for context, rheumatoid arthritis (RA). We conducted a retrospective cohort study using electronic health records data between June 2006 and June 2026. ICD codes were used to define populations of SpA-related diseases and RA. We estimated recorded baseline prevalence and crude incidence of HS, then separately performed 1:1 propensity-score matched comparisons of each disease with healthcare controls, matching for age, sex, BMI and comorbidities. The disease populations ranged from 55,407 to 429,647 individuals. Recorded HS prevalence was highest in psoriasis (0.65%), PsA (0.52%) and Crohn's disease (0.47%). Crude incidence was highest in Crohn's (187.4 per 100,000 person-years) and PsA (134.1 per 100,000 person-years). After matching, incidence was higher than in controls for PsA (incidence rate ratio [IRR] 1.63, 95% CI 1.41-1.88), Crohn's disease (2.02, 1.85-2.20), and ulcerative colitis (1.17, 1.04-1.32). Incidence was lower than controls in axSpA and RA. This study highlights a significant epidemiological association between HS and PsA and Crohn's disease. Clinicians providing care to these patient groups should consider enquiring about HS symptoms, although overall incidence rates are low. Further research is needed into the shared pathophysiology of HS and psoriatic disease.

items.title: Case Report: Delayed diagnosis of adult-onset Still's disease after sepsis-like acute liver failure with macrophage activation syndrome.
items.abstract: Adult-onset Still's disease (AOSD) is a rare systemic autoinflammatory disease characterized by heterogeneous and nonspecific clinical manifestations. It often requires differentiation from infectious diseases, malignancies, and other rheumatic autoimmune disorders, making early diagnosis challenging. Acute liver failure (ALF) is a rare but severe complication of AOSD. AOSD may also be complicated by macrophage activation syndrome (MAS), a severe hyperinflammatory condition that can cause multiorgan dysfunction and mimic sepsis, further complicating diagnosis and management. We report a 35-year-old woman with AOSD complicated by macrophage activation syndrome who initially presented with acute liver failure. Multiple pathogens were detected by metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS), leading to an initial misdiagnosis of sepsis. Over the following two years, the patient experienced recurrent episodes of fever, rash, arthralgia, and liver dysfunction. After comprehensive evaluation, the diagnosis of AOSD was established according to the Yamaguchi criteria, and MAS was diagnosed based on the HLH-2004 criteria and HScore. The patient achieved clinical remission after high-dose glucocorticoid therapy and remained stable during follow-up. This case highlights that AOSD complicated by MAS should be considered in patients with unexplained fever and acute liver failure, particularly those with hyperferritinemia, rash, and multisystem involvement. Even in the presence of evidence suggestive of infection, clinicians should remain vigilant for AOSD with MAS to avoid misdiagnosis and delayed treatment.

items.title: Total glucosides of paeony inhibits the differentiation and migration of intestinal mucosal immune Th17 cells in Sjogren's syndrome mice.
items.abstract: Sjogren's syndrome (SS) is marked by exocrine-gland infiltration and Th17-driven inflammation; low-bioavailability Total glucosides of paeony (TGP) shows efficacy yet unclear mechanisms. To investigate the role of intestinal mucosal immunity in SS pathogenesis and the effect of TGP on the differentiation and migration of Th17 in intestinal mucosal immunity. SS was induced in Peyer's patches (PPs)/mesenteric lymph nodes (MLNs)-deficient mice. Saliva/tear flow, gland histopathology, Th17-related cytokine mRNA and blood Th17 were assessed. Established SS mice were treated with 6-week TGP. Flow cytometry/RT-qPCR evaluated CD4 + T cell proliferation, dendritic cell (DC) activation, and Th17 differentiation, migration and homing in intestinal mucosal immunity, blood, exocrine glands. Immunofluorescence observed the migration of in vitro -polarized, CFSE-labeled Th17 cells to the submandibular glands (SMG). In vitro , naive CD4 + T cells from PPs/MLNs were cultured with cytokines or LPS-activated bone marrow DCs (BMDCs) to induce Th17 differentiation, with TGP incubated. CD4 + T cell proliferation, Th17 proportion and cytokine mRNA was determined. PPs- or MLNs-deficient SS mice showed no significant increase in SS manifestations or Th17 markers. In vivo , TGP inhibited CD4 + T cell proliferation, Th17 differentiation and DC activation/migration, blocking Th17 gland entry and gut homing by down-regulating CCR6/CCL20, CCR9/CCL25 and α4β7/MAdCAM-1 axis. Immunofluorescence results also clearly demonstrated that TGP significantly inhibited the migration of intestinal mucosa-derived Th17 cells to the SMG. In vitro , TGP left BMDC activation intact but sharply suppressed BMDC-driven Th17 differentiation by reducing proliferation and Th17 cytokines. TGP attenuates SS inflammation by inhibiting Th17 differentiation and migration from intestinal mucosal immunity to exocrine glands and their homing to intestinal mucosa.

items.title: Novel clustering approach to understanding distinct phenotypes of patients with systemic sclerosis.
items.abstract: Despite earlier clustering studies on systemic sclerosis (SSc), how clinical subgroups differ in disease burden, treatment and patient-physician dynamics remains unclear. This study applied a novel clustering method to identify clinical subgroups. Data were analysed from 1906 adults with SSc and their treating rheumatologists across the USA, France, Germany, Italy, Spain, UK and Japan (March-September 2022). Data were collected by Adelphi Real World as part of an independent survey titled the SSc I Disease Specific Programme, comprising data from the USA, France, Germany, Italy, Spain, UK and Japan. Physicians completed case record forms; patients completed self-reported questionnaires. Latent class clustering was conducted using five physician-reported variables: affected body areas, symptoms, severity, flares in the past 12 months and remission status. This was a non-interventional, observational, retrospective study. A cluster solution was selected based on model fit and clinical interpretability. We compared time to diagnosis, symptoms at diagnosis, postdiagnosis trajectories, physician management and patient treatment perspectives across clusters. We identified four clusters representing a gradient of disease severity, with all clusters comprising >75% females. Clusters 1/2 comprised younger patients with fewer concomitant conditions; Clusters 3/4 showed greater internal organ involvement and disease severity. Raynaud's phenomenon (RP) was the most frequent first symptom (physician-reported: 73%-85%; patient-reported: 63%-79%), but those with first symptoms other than RP were diagnosed faster (mean 1.06 vs 1.62 years). Musculoskeletal involvement was most pronounced in Clusters 2/4. Postdiagnosis (3.7-7.2 years), the number of symptoms and affected body areas decreased in Cluster 1, increased in Cluster 4 and remained relatively stable in Clusters 2/3. Improvement in disease progression within the first 2 years postdiagnosis was more often reported in Clusters 1/2 vs 3/4 (33%-34% vs 8%-20%). Most patients across clusters reported that the main benefit they wanted from treatment was to get rid of the disease. This analysis improves understanding of SSc beyond limited/diffuse subtypes. Musculoskeletal involvement emerged as a contributor to SSc burden, supporting its integration into monitoring/stratification strategies for earlier identification of high-risk patients.

items.title: Ikaros degradation by Iberdomide correlates with normalization of cytokines in Th cells of patients with systemic lupus erythematosus.
items.abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus is sustained by dysfunctional Th cells that amplify autoreactive B-cell responses. Iberdomide, a cereblon modulator that degrades Ikaros and Aiolos, has shown clinical activity in lupus, yet its T cell-centric mechanism remains incompletely defined. Here, using purified Th cells and a PBMC-based T-B cell activation assay, we asked whether targeted degradation of Ikaros reprograms pathogenic T-cell circuitry and constrains B-cell hyperactivity. At baseline, lupus Th cells exhibited the canonical pattern of diminished IL-2 and TNF-α levels, with enrichment of Th2-associated cytokines and elevated IL-6 and IL-9 levels. Iberdomide restored IL-2 and TNF-α and suppressed Th2-associated cytokines, IL-6, and IL-9 across secreted and single-cell readouts. Although the relative frequency of CXCR5+PD-1+ Tfh-like cells increased, ICOS expression decreased; IL-21 increased numerically but not significantly in total CD4 T cells. In the PBMC-based T-B cell activation assay, iberdomide reduced B-cell recovery, plasmablast-like differentiation, and anti-dsDNA levels. Interdonor variability in cytokine modulation tracked more strongly with Ikaros than Aiolos. These findings show iberdomide alters lupus T-cell cytokine networks and is associated with reduced B-cell responses.

items.title: JQ1 Inhibits the Hyperproliferation and Aggressiveness of Fibroblast-Like Synoviocytes in Rheumatoid Arthritis via Regulating IL7R.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune bone disease. BRD4 is implicated in the pathogenesis of bone disorders. This study aimed to investigate the effects of a BRD4 inhibitor JQ1 on RA. Fibroblast-like synoviocytes (FLS) were exposed to TNF-α to establish an in vitro RA model. mRNA levels were detected using RT-qPCR. Protein expression was assessed by Western blot. The behaviors of FLS were analyzed using CCK-8, EdU, wound scratch, and transwell assays. We found that LPS exposure promoted an inflammatory response in FLS, as well as mediated cell proliferation and migration. Interestingly, JQ1 inhibited the inflammatory response and the morbidity of FLS. Mechanistically, targeting BRD4 by JQ1 inhibited acetylation modification for H3K27 on IL7R promoter, downregulating the expression of IL7R. However, IL7R overexpression reversed the effects of JQ1 and promoted the inflammatory response and the morbidity of FLS. JQ1 inhibits the inflammatory response, proliferation, and migration of RA FLS via downregulating IL7R. Therefore, JQ1 exerts protective effects on RA.

items.title: Parthenolide ameliorated gout-like inflammation by inhibiting activation of NLRP3 inflammasome.
items.abstract: Crystals of monosodium urate (MSU) are the cause of gout, a common inflammatory disease. Parthenolide (Par), sesquiterpene lactone, derived from feverfew ( Pyrethrum parthenium ), possesses potent analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and anticancer properties. However, it remains elusive whether and how Par modulates gout. This research was designed to explore the therapeutic effect and mechanism of Par in acute gout. Chondrocytes from rat knee joint and mouse peritoneal macrophages (MPMs) were stimulated by lipopolysaccharide (LPS) plus MSU. Combination of yeast extract (YE) with oxygen oxyazine (OXO) was administered to mice to simulate hyperuricemia. MSU crystals were injected into the mice's paws or subcutaneously into the mice's backs to establish acute gouty models. Par blocked the activation of NOD-Like Receptor Pyrin Domains 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome by reducing the expression and release of inflammatory mediators in gouty mice and LPS plus MSU-stimulated MPMs, LPS plus MSU-stimulated chondrocytes as well. Par also promoted phagocytosis abilities of MPMs and chondrocytes to reduce inflammation. In addition, Par dose-dependently reduced the serum levels of uric acid (UA), xanthine oxidase (XOD), creatinine (CRE), and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and ameliorated renal injury in mice with hyperuricemia. Par ameliorated uric acid metabolism disorders of hyperuricemia, and improved acute gout-like inflammation through the inhibition of NLRP3 inflammasome activation, indicating that Par may be a promising candidate for gout-targeted therapy.

items.title: Selenium nanozymes effectively treat rheumatoid arthritis by specifically activating selenoproteins to block oxidative damage and cGAS-STING signaling pathway.
items.abstract: Redox imbalance has become an important factor in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) progression, previous studies showed selenium nanozymes (Se NPs) effectively treated RA by restoring redox. However, the process of Se NPs regulates RA, especially the mechanism of Se NPs activates selenoproteins in inhibiting inflammation remains unclear. Herein, the redox imbalance in RA patients was first analyzed, and selenoproteins associated with macrophage inflammation were identified via mRNA profiling. Subsequently, the synthesized Se NPs with glutathione peroxidase (GPX)-like activity as a supplement, and it was found that Se NPs specially upregulate selenoproteins in macrophages applied to in vitro and in vivo models, furthermore combined with GPX-like activity, Se NPs quickly eliminated reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (RONS), restored redox homeostasis in RA, and alleviated symptoms of RA by effectively inhibiting macrophage inflammation. The mechanistic study showed that Se NPs effectively prevent mitochondrial and nDNA damage by specifically activating selenoproteins, blocking the interaction between DNA and cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS), and restraining the activation of cGAS-stimulator of interferon genes (STING) and nuclear factor kappa-B (NF- κ B) pathway, thus effectively suppressing macrophage inflammation and treating RA. Therefore, this study reveals the mechanism by which Se NPs inhibit macrophage inflammation, providing a new potential therapeutic target for treating inflammatory diseases.

items.title: A mechanistic quantitative systems pharmacology framework enriched by multiscale data enables model-informed translational development of mesenchymal stem cell therapy in lupus nephritis.
items.abstract: Lupus nephritis (LN) is a complex autoimmune disease and mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), given their unique immune-modulatory potential, have emerged as a promising route for treating LN. Understanding the multiscale dynamic LN-MSC interactions and selecting the optimal clinical design for MSCs is critical to enhance their therapeutic potential and achieve meaningful benefit-risk differentiation in patients. To guide MSC clinical development, we constructed the first mechanistic quantitative systems pharmacology model of LN pathophysiology that integrated multimodal preclinical-clinical data, with detailed illustration of standard-of-care immunosuppressant pharmacology and physiologically-based biodistribution and therapeutic mechanisms of MSCs. We created model-based virtual LN patients that well captured clinical interpatient heterogeneity and were validated by numerous sets of clinical efficacy readouts, including first-hand results from our investigator-initiated trial testing MSCs in LN patients. We used this computational framework and identified that a spaced two-infusion MSC dosing strategy would yield optimal clinical response in LN patients, which directly informed the phase 2 design of a novel MSC therapy. Modeling analyses further identified that CXCL10 in combination with proteinuria are potential predictive biomarkers that could boost clinical renal response to MSCs. These results demonstrated the exceptional importance of our QSP framework in driving MSC clinical development for LN patients.

items.title: Recurrent Immune-Mediated Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura in the Setting of Suspected Sjögren's Syndrome.
items.abstract: A 70-year-old African American female with a past history of relapsing/remitting thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), hypertensive retinopathy, and breast cancer was evaluated in the rheumatology clinic for a possible autoimmune rheumatic disease. Earlier, she had followed up with a community rheumatologist who diagnosed her with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and Sjögren syndrome (SS). She was being treated with hydroxychloroquine, but this was discontinued after her hospitalization for a TTP flare. Investigations revealed the presence of anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA) and anti-SSA antibodies. Anti-double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) and anti-Smith antibodies were not present. Her main complaints were dry eyes and dry mouth, and there were no rashes, mouth sores, alopecia, serositis or polyarthritis. Although she had a positive ANA, the available clinical and serologic documentation did not establish sufficient additional criteria to fulfill the 2019 European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology/American College of Rheumatology (EULAR/ACR) classification criteria for SLE. Her relapsing TTP was treated with multiple courses of rituximab and plasmapheresis with ADAMTS13 level monitoring. Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) was added as a steroid-sparing immunosuppressive agent in the setting of recurrent immune-mediated TTP, ongoing corticosteroid exposure, and concomitant autoimmune features suggestive of Sjögren disease. Thereafter, the patient remained stable without another documented TTP relapse during follow-up. This temporal association does not establish that MMF prevented TTP relapse. This case report emphasizes an interesting association between suspected Sjögren disease and recurrent TTP and highlights the diagnostic and therapeutic challenges of managing recurrent TTP in the setting of systemic autoimmune features.

items.title: Takayasu Arteritis Presenting With Hypotension and Chronic Cerebral Infarctions in a Young Woman: A Case Report.
items.abstract: Takayasu arteritis (TAK) is a rare large-vessel vasculitis that predominantly affects young women and can present with nonspecific symptoms, making early diagnosis challenging. Neurological manifestations may occur secondary to involvement of the carotid and vertebral arteries and can result in cerebral ischemia. We report the case of a 28-year-old woman who presented with recurrent dizziness, presyncope, palpitations, visual disturbances, and persistent hypotension. Initial neuroimaging demonstrated indeterminate supratentorial hypodensities, while subsequent magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed multiple chronic cerebral infarcts involving the bilateral centrum semiovale and an abnormal flow void of the right internal carotid artery. Further computed tomography angiography demonstrated extensive large-vessel disease, including marked narrowing and wall thickening of the bilateral common carotid and subclavian arteries, critical stenosis of the right internal carotid artery, and narrowing of both vertebral arteries. Clinical examination revealed absent peripheral pulses and carotid and subclavian bruits, raising suspicion for large-vessel vasculitis. Following multidisciplinary assessment, the combination of the patient's age, chronic cerebral ischemic changes, extensive arterial disease, pulse deficits, and vascular bruits was considered consistent with TAK. She was treated with intravenous methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisolone and aspirin, with significant improvement in her presenting symptoms. This case highlights the importance of considering TAK in young patients presenting with unexplained neurological symptoms, hypotension, or chronic cerebral ischemic lesions, particularly when vascular examination reveals pulse deficits or arterial bruits. It also emphasizes the value of comprehensive vascular imaging and multidisciplinary assessment in identifying extensive large-vessel involvement.

items.title: Large, Life-Threatening Right Ventricular and Pulmonary Artery Thrombus Revealing Antiphospholipid Syndrome: The Role of Risk Stratification and Thrombolytic Therapy.
items.abstract: Right ventricular thrombus in the setting of acute pulmonary embolism is an uncommon and potentially life-threatening finding associated with a high risk of hemodynamic deterioration. The optimal management remains controversial, particularly in patients with an extensive thrombotic burden but without overt hemodynamic instability. We report a case of a patient presenting with an extensive thrombus occupying the right ventricle and extending into the pulmonary artery. Multimodality imaging demonstrated a significant thrombotic burden with right ventricular involvement and confirmed acute pulmonary embolism. Echocardiographic assessment revealed right ventricular thrombus and signs of right ventricular pressure overload. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging findings, and right ventricular involvement, the patient was classified as having intermediate-high-risk pulmonary embolism. Given the large mobile right ventricular thrombus with pulmonary arterial extension, profound hypoxemia (oxygen saturation: 54%) on room air, and severe tachypnea (45 breaths/min), systemic thrombolysis was considered despite the absence of hemodynamic collapse. After multidisciplinary discussion, an individualized treatment decision was made to administer reduced-dose tenecteplase (0.25 mg/kg; 15 mg). Marked clinical improvement was observed within 24 hours, with no major bleeding complications. Further investigations revealed antiphospholipid syndrome as the underlying prothrombotic condition. At three-month follow-up, the patient remained clinically stable, with a marked reduction in the residual right ventricular thrombus and resolution of the pulmonary trunk thrombus. This case highlights the importance of early echocardiographic identification of right ventricular thrombus in patients with pulmonary embolism and the role of multimodality imaging in therapeutic decision-making. It also illustrates the potential role of reduced-dose systemic thrombolysis in selected patients with intermediate-high-risk pulmonary embolism and extensive intracardiac thrombotic burden. Recognition of the underlying prothrombotic disorder is essential for guiding long-term anticoagulation and preventing recurrent thromboembolic events.

items.title: Patterns of the gut microbiota and metabolome as potential biomarkers associated with influenza vaccine immunogenicity in systemic lupus erythematosus: a cross-sectional observational pilot study.
items.abstract: Immunogenicity to influenza vaccination is often impaired in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). The role of the gut microbiota and its metabolic output in modulating this response remains underexplored. This study is the first to explore gut microbiota patterns and metabolites in response to influenza vaccination in patients with SLE. A cross-sectional observational pilot study was conducted at Ramathibodi Hospital between May 2021 and July 2022. Participants with SLE who had received either a boosted dose or a standard dose of a quadrivalent influenza vaccine were enrolled. We analyzed fecal 16 S rDNA and metabolomic profiles using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry to identify signatures associated with seroconversion (determined using the hemagglutination inhibition assay). A total of 62 participants with SLE participated in the study, and 61 fecal samples were submitted for metabolomic analysis. Most participants were female (58/62, 93.6%). The median ages in the standard and booster dose groups were 35.5 (interquartile range 28-42.5) and 34 (25-43) years, respectively (P = 0.878). The overall gut microbiota patterns were similar in both groups; however, the genus Bacteroides was significantly associated with seroconversion to A(H1N1) and A(H3N2) (P < 0.05). Metabolomic analysis identified upregulation of 1,5-anhydro-D-glucitol and L-cysteic acid in seroconverters, whereas neopterin was significantly elevated in nonresponders, furthermore, several bacterial taxa were correlated with these metabolites. The level of immunosuppressive treatment and the use of antimicrobials for prophylaxis against opportunistic infections affected influenza immunogenicity in this study population. Some metabolites also appeared to be linked to vaccine immunogenicity, although the underlying mechanism is unclear. Our findings identify specific gut microbial taxa and fecal metabolites, particularly 1,5-anhydro-D-glucitol, which are significantly associated with influenza vaccine immunogenicity in SLE patients. These results suggest that the gut-immune axis may play a modulatory role in vaccine responses and may provide potential non-invasive biomarkers that can identify patients at risk of suboptimal influenza protection.

items.title: Outcomes of arthrocentesis and arthroscopy in the management of TMJ involvement in juvenile idiopathic arthritis: a retrospective analysis.
items.abstract: Temporomandibular joint (TMJ) involvement in juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is common, frequently underrecognized, and may progress despite minimal symptoms. Untreated TMJ arthritis has been associated with pain, functional limitation, and dentofacial growth disturbance, supporting early identification and intervention even in clinically subtle disease. The role of minimally invasive TMJ procedures remains incompletely defined. The aim of this study was to evaluate patient-reported and clinical outcomes following TMJ arthrocentesis or arthroscopy in patients with symptomatic TMJ involvement associated with JIA. We retrospectively evaluated 45 patients with JIA who underwent TMJ arthrocentesis or arthroscopy between 2014 and 2023. The cohort was 96% female, with a mean age of 15.7 years at first intervention (range, 6.0-23.0 years). TMJ arthrocentesis was performed in 27% of study subjects and arthroscopy in 73%; intra-articular corticosteroid injection was administered in 80%. Outcomes included the patient-completed 20-item Jaw Functional Limitation Scale (JFLS-20), pain measures including the Characteristic Pain Index (CPI) derived from the Graded Chronic Pain Scale, and maximal interincisal opening (MIO) at early (0-3 months), intermediate (3-9 months), and late (9-24 months) follow-up. Regression analyses identified improvement predictors and need for additional surgical intervention. Minimally invasive TMJ procedures were associated with significant early and intermediate improvements in function, pain, and mouth opening (p < 0.05). These benefits diminished over time, and recurrent symptoms were common, with 20 study subjects (44%) requiring additional procedures during follow-up. Procedure type and JIA subtype were not associated with outcomes. MRI-confirmed synovitis, greater baseline functional limitation, DMARD use, and younger age predicted greater early improvement. Higher number of tender sites predicted both early pain improvement and increased likelihood of re-intervention. Minimally invasive TMJ procedures provide meaningful but often temporary symptomatic relief in JIA-associated TMJ arthritis. High re-intervention rates likely reflect the complex and recurrent nature of TMJ symptoms in this population. These findings support the selective adjunctive use of local TMJ interventions within a multidisciplinary, systemically focused treatment strategy aimed at mitigating symptomatic burden and potential long-term sequelae.

items.title: Sustained pain improvement and IL-12-related biomarker changes in rheumatoid arthritis patients initiating baricitinib or TNF inhibitor therapy.
items.abstract: The Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor baricitinib has demonstrated analgesic effects that may extend beyond anti-inflammatory mechanisms. This study investigated longitudinal pain trajectories and their association with interleukin (IL)-6 and IL-12 changes in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) initiating baricitinib or tumour necrosis factor inhibitor (TNFi) therapy. In this single-centre prospective study, 60 patients with RA initiating baricitinib (n = 29) or TNFi therapy (n = 31) were followed at baseline, 2 weeks and 3 months. Healthy donors (n = 15) served as a biomarker reference. IL-6, IL-12p40, and IL-12p70 were measured using Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA) and multiplex technology. Pain was assessed using numerical rating scales, and disease activity and function using 28-joint Disease Activity Score-erythrocyte sedimentation rate and Health Assessment Questionnaire Disability Index. Analyses were within-group and exploratory; adjusted mixed-effects models assessed between-group trajectories. Within both groups, disease activity, function, and all 3 pain domains improved significantly over 3 months. Under baricitinib, average pain and swollen joint count (SJC) improved further between 2 weeks and 3 months, whereas TNFi showed earlier improvement at 2 weeks. IL-6, IL-12p40, and IL-12p70 showed within-group reductions under baricitinib, reaching significance at 3 months. Adjusted models showed no robust between-group differences. In this small prospective pilot cohort, both therapies were associated with early, clinically relevant pain improvement, with continued improvement in average pain and SJC under baricitinib. This sustained response was accompanied by within-group reductions in IL-6 and, notably, the IL-12 subunits, a JAK/tyrosine kinase(TYK)-linked pathway that has been less explored in relation to RA pain. These exploratory observations are hypothesis-generating and warrant confirmation in larger, adequately powered studies.

items.title: Deletion of a rheumatoid arthritis risk enhancer in mouse disrupts Bim expression and immune homeostasis.
items.abstract: This study aimed to characterise the in vivo function of a murine regulatory region syntenic to the human rheumatoid arthritis (RA)-associated enhancer at the ACOXL locus and its role in immunity. Using CRISPR-Cas9, we generated the Bim-eΔ mouse model by excising a 15 kb genomic region syntenic to the human RA-associated locus tagged by rs13401811 from C57BL/6J zygotes. Bim expression was assessed by quantitative polymerase chain reaction. Thymocytes and splenocytes were profiled by flow cytometry, and whole-spleen RNA-seq was used to define transcriptional changes. Immune responses were tested using a Trichuris muris infection model and an antigen-induced arthritis (AIA) protocol. Bim-eΔ mice show reduced Bim expression vs wild-type counterparts. This indicates that Bim is a transcriptional target of this region. Enhancer loss was correlated with differences in T cell proportions across age- and sex-stratified cohorts consistent with altered thymic selection. Splenic T and B cells were altered, and the transcriptome skewed toward inflammation. Bim-eΔ and wild-type mice mounted comparable responses to T. muris , whereas Bim-eΔ mice developed a severe adverse response during the sensitisation phase of the AIA protocol. A murine noncoding regulatory region modulates Bim expression and immunity in vivo . Enhancer deletion altered the splenic transcriptional profile and lymphocyte composition while revealing a context-dependent phenotype upon inflammatory in vivo challenge. These findings support a role for RA-associated regulatory architecture in shaping immunity and point to BIM regulation as a potential therapeutic lever for restoring immune balance.

items.title: Beyond Traditional Risk: Does Systemic Inflammation Drive Accelerated Atherosclerosis in Rheumatoid Arthritis?
items.abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the primary cause of morbidity and mortality in individuals with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and other rheumatic diseases (RDs), contributing to an approximate 50% increased cardiovascular risk relative to the general population. In addition to conventional cardiovascular risk factors, disease-specific processes such as chronic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and immunological dysregulation substantially accelerate atherosclerosis. This thorough analysis brings together the most recent information on how to measure cardiovascular risk, how to understand the underlying causes of RA and other rheumatic diseases, and how to treat them all together. In RA, long-term inflammation throughout the body causes atherosclerosis through several different mechanisms that are not related to common risk factors. To lower the risk of heart disease, rheumatologists, cardiologists, dietitians, physiotherapists, and immunologists must all work together. Evidence supports the targeting of disease activity, the management of conventional cardiovascular risk factors such as hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, and the use of non-pharmacological therapies.

items.title: Sleep Disorders in Patients with Systemic Sclerosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
items.abstract: Background : Systemic sclerosis is a rare autoimmune disease associated with substantial morbidity and reduced quality of life. Sleep disturbance has been reported with variable frequency in patients with systemic sclerosis, though its prevalence remains incompletely characterised. Objective : This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to estimate the pooled prevalence of sleep disorders in patients with systemic sclerosis. Methods : Six databases were searched up to 15 February 2026 without language restriction. Studies reporting sleep outcomes in adults with systemic sclerosis were eligible. Prevalence estimates were pooled using a logit transformation with a random-effects model and Hartung-Knapp correction. Heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic. Publication bias was evaluated with Egger's test and the trim-and-fill method. This review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251152354). Results : Twenty-three studies totalling 1,487 patients were included across all analyses. Eleven studies (820 patients) contributed to the primary meta-analysis of poor sleep quality assessed by the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. The pooled prevalence of poor sleep quality was 76.49% (95% CI 66.62 to 84.13%), with moderate to substantial heterogeneity (I² = 70.1%) and a 95% prediction interval of 49.66% to 91.47%, indicating that the true prevalence may range from approximately half to nearly all patients across different SSc populations. Five studies (346 patients) contributed to the obstructive sleep apnea meta-analysis, yielding a pooled prevalence of 40.30% (95% CI 25.56 to 57.04%, I² = 71.8%) with a 95% prediction interval of 13.95% to 73.75%. Five additional studies were included in a qualitative synthesis only, and three randomised controlled trials addressed sleep interventions. Egger's test identified possible funnel plot asymmetry. After trim-and-fill adjustment, four studies were imputed and the corrected estimate was 69.62% (95% CI 57.33 to 79.63%), somewhat lower than the primary estimate, suggesting that the primary estimate may be modestly influenced by publication bias. The certainty of evidence was rated as low according to GRADE. Conclusion : Available evidence suggests that sleep disorders may affect approximately three quarters of patients with systemic sclerosis when assessed by the PSQI, and obstructive sleep apnea may affect more than one third when evaluated by objective tools. These estimates carry low GRADE certainty and wide prediction intervals, and should not be interpreted as definitive prevalence figures. Larger prospective studies and well-powered randomised trials are needed to establish more precise estimates and to evaluate targeted sleep interventions in this population.

items.title: Association of UGT1A9-2152C>T gene polymorphism with mycophenolic acid response in Indonesian patients with lupus nephritis.
items.abstract: Mycophenolic acid (MPA) is a key immunosuppressant for lupus nephritis (LN), yet therapeutic response varies widely among individuals. Genetic variation in UGT1A9, particularly the -2152C>T promoter polymorphism, may influence MPA metabolism and exposure. Most existing pharmacogenomic studies have focused on solid organ transplant recipients, while evidence in autoimmune diseases, especially among Southeast Asian populations, remains limited. This study aimed to evaluate the association between the UGT1A9-2152C>T promoter polymorphism and MPA treatment response in Indonesian patients with LN. A case-control study was conducted among 74 patients with LN receiving MPA therapy. Treatment response was classified as responders (n = 45) or non-responders (n = 29) based on the Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Disease Activity Responder Index-50 (SRI-50). Genotyping of the UGT1A9-2152C>T polymorphism was performed using polymerase chain reaction-restriction fragment length polymorphism. No significant differences in genotype frequencies or allele distribution were observed between responders and non-responders (P > 0.05). The T allele frequency was 11.5% and was not significantly associated with treatment response. UGT1A9-2152C>T showed no significant association with MPA response in Indonesian LN patients. These findings provide initial local pharmacogenomic evidence and underscore the need for larger multi-gene studies to support genotype-guided MPA therapy.

items.title: Axial spondyloarthropathy with peripheral joint involvement mimicking gout on ultrasound: A case of double contour sign pitfall.
items.abstract: Axial spondyloarthropathy (axSpA) may present with peripheral joint involvement, which makes the diagnosis more challenging when axial symptoms are unrecognized. In this report, a 66-year-old man presented with chronic left knee pain and swelling as the initially recognized musculoskeletal manifestation of axSpA. A double contour sign (DCS)-like appearance near the fibular head and a DCS at the first metatarsophalangeal joint initially suggested gout. Subsequent evaluations, including dual-energy CT, sacroiliac joint CT and MRI, and HLA-B27 testing, led to a diagnosis of axSpA with peripheral joint involvement. This case highlights diagnostic pitfalls in musculoskeletal ultrasound, particularly the gout-specific DCS. It also emphasizes the importance of correlating imaging findings with clinical symptoms and pain distribution.

items.title: Genetic liability to systemic lupus erythematosus and autoimmune thyroid diseases: evidence from a bidirectional mendelian randomization study.
items.abstract: Previous observational studies imply a potential link between systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and autoimmune thyroid disease (AITD), although they are susceptible to confounding factors. This study aims to assess the genetic evidence for a potential causal association between SLE and AITD using a bidirectional and multivariable two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis. We retrieved datasets for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), autoimmune thyroiditis (AT), autoimmune hyperthyroidism, and autoimmune hypothyroidism from European population-based databases, and data for Graves' disease (GD) from Biobank Japan (BBJ). Instrumental variables (IVs) related to exposure were selected for the Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis. Sensitivity tests, including horizontal pleiotropy and heterogeneity assessments, were conducted to ensure result reliability, and the analysis outcomes were visualized. Bonferroni correction was applied to the 8 primary exposure-outcome pairs (corrected significance threshold p < 0.00625). The use of a Japanese GWAS dataset for GD alongside predominantly European datasets for other phenotypes represents a methodological limitation due to potential cross-ancestry differences in linkage disequilibrium structure and allele frequencies. Genetic variants linked to SLE, AT, GD, autoimmune hyperthyroidism, and autoimmune hypothyroidism were utilized as IVs. MR analysis was performed using data from 5201 SLE cases and 9066 controls; 244 AT cases and 187,684 controls; 2176 GD cases and 210,277 controls; 962 autoimmune hyperthyroidism cases and 172,976 controls; 22,997 autoimmune hypothyroidism cases and 175,475 controls. In the primary IVW analysis, genetic liability to SLE was associated with increased risks of AT (OR = 1.136, 95% CI 1.006-1.284, p = 0.040) and autoimmune hypothyroidism (OR = 1.036, 95% CI 1.004-1.070, p = 0.025). Genetically predicted autoimmune hyperthyroidism is associated with an increased risk of SLE in both univariable (OR = 1.905, 95% CI 1.195-3.037, p = 0.007) and multivariable (OR = 1.381, 95% CI 1.042-1.830, p = 0.024) MR analyses. However, these associations did not remain statistically significant after Bonferroni correction for 8 tested exposure-outcome pairs (corrected significance threshold: p < 0.00625). Sensitivity analysis showed limited evidence of horizontal pleiotropy, though significant heterogeneity was detected for several exposure-outcome pairs (see Fig. 5). Mendelian randomization analysis suggests that genetic liability to SLE is associated with a potential increased risk of AT and autoimmune hypothyroidism, and genetic liability to autoimmune hyperthyroidism is associated with a possible increased risk of SLE in European populations. These findings are based on genetic instruments and should be interpreted as genetic evidence consistent with potential causal effects rather than definitive proof of causality. The observed associations have relatively modest effect sizes and reflect lifelong genetic liability; they should not be equated with the clinical epidemiological risk among patients with established disease. Their clinical relevance requires further validation in large-scale prospective clinical studies. The mixed ancestry of GWAS datasets and the presence of significant heterogeneity are important limitations. Key Points • This study systematically evaluated the bidirectional genetic associations between SLE and distinct AITD subtypes via a comprehensive bidirectional and multivariable two-sample MR design. • Genetic liability to SLE was genetically associated with an increased risk of AT and autoimmune hypothyroidism in European populations. • Autoimmune hyperthyroidism was identified as a potential genetic risk factor for SLE, validated by both univariable and multivariable MR analyses. • The findings provide genetic evidence for understanding the shared genetic architecture and potential causal associations between SLE and AITD subtypes. However, given the modest effect sizes and the distinction between genetic liability and clinical disease, they do not currently support routine targeted thyroid comorbidity screening in all SLE patients without further clinical validation.
