items.title: Clinical Phenotype, Treatment Exposure, Treat-to-Target Status, and Longitudinal Outcomes in Juvenile-Onset Systemic Lupus Erythematosus: A Single-Center Retrospective Cohort Study.
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Treat-to-target assessment is central to the management of juvenile-onset systemic lupus erythematosus (jSLE). We primarily evaluated last-visit childhood lupus low disease activity state (cLLDAS) status and its limiting components, and secondarily described clinical phenotype, treatment exposure, and outcomes. Methods: This retrospective single-center cohort included 54 patients with jSLE followed during 2020-2025; one patient who died 10 days after diagnosis was excluded from last-visit analyses, and the remaining 53 had at least 6 months of follow-up. The Paediatric Rheumatology European Society (PReS)-endorsed cLLDAS definition was applied at the last visit using a retrospectively assigned physician global assessment (PGA). Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Disease Activity Index 2000 (SLEDAI-2K) and laboratory values at diagnosis and the latest assessment were compared descriptively. Results: Median age at diagnosis was 15.0 years, and median follow-up was 34.6 months (IQR 21.2-70.6). Biopsy-proven lupus nephritis occurred in 29.6% (class IV, 13/16). Median SLEDAI-2K was 8.0 at diagnosis and 4.0 at the latest assessment. At the last visit, 29/53 patients (54.7%; 95% CI 40.4-68.4) were in cLLDAS, and 32/53 (60.4%) met the SLEDAI-2K and glucocorticoid components; of 24 patients outside the target, 17 had SLEDAI-2K > 4 and 7 exceeded the glucocorticoid ceiling (both in 3). Conservative minimum rates of flare, infection-related hospitalization, and intensive care unit admission were 5.6, 5.2, and 1.4 per 100 patient-years, respectively; one early death occurred. Conclusions: Just over half of the patients were in cLLDAS at the last visit, with residual disease activity as the main barrier, followed by glucocorticoid dose. These observational data reflect outcomes within the available follow-up period and cannot establish treatment effectiveness or long-term prognosis.

items.title: Sexual Function After Corrective Spinal Osteotomy in Female Patients with Ankylosing Spondylitis: A Retrospective Single-Center Case Series.
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) may cause progressive spinal rigidity and kyphotic deformity, with consequences for physical function, quality of life, and sexual health. Data regarding sexual function following corrective spinal osteotomy in women with AS are limited. This study aimed to describe radiological and functional changes and to explore within-patient changes in sexual function following corrective spinal osteotomy. Methods: This retrospective single-center case series analyzed prospectively maintained data from female patients with AS who underwent single-level pedicle subtraction osteotomy for thoracolumbar kyphosis between 2015 and 2024. The primary outcome was the change in total Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI) score from baseline to the standardized two-year assessment. Secondary outcomes (analyzed as exploratory, without adjustment for multiplicity) included FSFI domains, Visual Analog Scale, Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Functional Index, and radiological parameters. Sexual-activity frequency, time to resumption of sexual activity, and preferred coital position were also recorded. Paired outcomes were analyzed using the exact Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and exploratory radiological-FSFI associations using Spearman's correlation with false-discovery-rate adjustment. Results: Eleven patients with complete two-year data were included. Significant postoperative changes were observed in several sagittal alignment parameters, as well as in Visual Analog Scale (VAS) and Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Functional Index (BASFI) scores. Total FSFI and the desire, arousal, orgasm, and satisfaction domains increased, whereas lubrication and pain did not change significantly. A descriptive shift toward higher-frequency sexual activity and different preferred coital positions was also observed. Radiological-FSFI correlations were interpreted cautiously because of the small sample and multiple comparisons. Conclusions: In this small exploratory cohort, postoperative assessment was associated with improved radiological alignment, pain, physical function, and several domains of self-reported sexual function. These findings represent within-patient changes and exploratory associations and do not establish a causal effect of spinal osteotomy on sexual function or a specific safe interval for resumption of sexual activity. Larger prospective studies are needed to confirm these observations.

items.title: Area-Level Rurality and Documented Musculoskeletal Symptom Presentation at Rheumatoid Arthritis Diagnosis Among Older Adults in Rural Japan: A Cross-Sectional Study.
items.abstract: Background: Recognizing rheumatoid arthritis (RA) in older adults is challenging because clinical presentations are heterogeneous and musculoskeletal symptoms may be attributed to aging or other conditions. Rural context may influence symptom recognition, healthcare-seeking, and diagnostic pathways. We examined whether area-level rurality was associated with musculoskeletal symptoms documented at RA diagnosis among older adults in rural Japan. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of 221 patients aged ≥65 years diagnosed with RA at a rural community hospital in Japan between 2016 and 2021. Area-level rurality was measured using the Rurality Index for Japan (RIJ). The primary outcome was documentation of hand, wrist, foot, or ankle symptoms at diagnosis. Logistic regression was used to examine the association between RIJ and the primary outcome. The primary adjusted model included age, sex, and Charlson Comorbidity Index. Results: Among 221 patients, 106 (48.0%) had documented hand, wrist, foot, or ankle symptoms. RIJ scores were higher among patients with these documented symptoms than among those without them (70.0 vs. 64.8; p = 0.004), and the interval from symptom onset to the study-hospital consultation was longer (48.5 vs. 28.0 days; p < 0.001). Each 10-point increase in RIJ was associated with higher odds of documented hand, wrist, foot, or ankle symptoms in the primary adjusted model (OR 1.30, 95% CI 1.07-1.57; p = 0.008). Exploratory sequential models incorporating consultation timing, CRP, and anti-CCP antibody levels yielded similar estimates. Sensitivity analysis accounting for clustering by residential postal-code area did not materially alter the association. Conclusions: Greater area-level rurality was modestly associated with the joint symptom pattern documented at RA diagnosis among older adults in this rural healthcare system. The findings should be interpreted as reflecting differences in documented clinical presentation within a diagnostic pathway rather than as evidence of a distinct rural RA phenotype. In rural settings, clinicians should systematically assess musculoskeletal symptoms in older adults with suspected inflammatory arthritis while remaining attentive to atypical presentations. Prospective multicenter studies using standardized joint assessments and direct individual-level measures of healthcare accessibility are needed to clarify how rural context relates to symptom recognition, healthcare-seeking, referral, and RA diagnosis.

items.title: Exploratory Risk Assessment of Cardiovascular Diseases Using Antiphospholipid Antibody-Related Scores in Patients with ANCA-Associated Vasculitis.
items.abstract: Background: Antiphospholipid antibodies have been found in patients with antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis (AAV). This study aimed to evaluate the accuracy of the global antiphospholipid syndrome score (GAPSS) derivatives in predicting cardiovascular diseases in Korean patients with AAV, and to derive a simple candidate index for cardiovascular diseases. Methods: This was a retrospective cohort study including 170 patients with AAV. The adjusted GAPSS (aGAPSS), aGAPSS specific for cardiovascular diseases (aGAPSScvd), and aGAPSS for Korean patients with APS (aGAPSS [KAPS]) were calculated in each patient. The cardiovascular diseases were defined as cerebrovascular accident (CVA) or acute coronary syndrome (ACS). The accuracy of each index was assessed by estimating the area under the curve (AUC). An exploratory multivariable Cox proportional hazards model with a backward elimination method was performed to derive a candidate index. Covariates consisting the aGAPSScvd were included in the model. Results: The AUCs of the aGAPSS, aGAPSScvd, and aGAPSS (KAPS) for CVA were 0.507 ( p = 0.926), 0.531 ( p = 0.676), and 0.493 ( p = 0.923), respectively. The AUCs of the aGAPSS, aGAPSScvd, and aGAPSS (KAPS) for ACS were 0.613 ( p = 0.441), 0.752 ( p = 0.086), and 0.796 ( p = 0.043), respectively. The exploratory multivariable model revealed a candidate index, aGAPSScvd for ACS in Korean patients with AAV (aGAPSScvd [KAAV]) = 2 × lupus anticoagulant (LA) + 2 × obesity. The AUC of the aGAPSScvd (KAAV) in predicting ACS was 0.843 ( p = 0.019). Conclusions: The two-item candidate index aGAPSScvd (KAAV), consisting of LA and obesity, showed discriminatory ability for ACS, which warrants further validation in larger studies.

items.title: Association of Anti-TNF Therapy with Ventricular Repolarization Indices in Patients with Rheumatoid Arthritis: A Longitudinal Electrocardiographic Study.
items.abstract: Background: Patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) have an increased risk of cardiovascular morbidity that cannot be fully explained by traditional cardiovascular risk factors alone. Chronic systemic inflammation has been implicated in myocardial electrical remodeling, yet the effect of anti-tumor necrosis factor (anti-TNF) therapy on ventricular repolarization remains insufficiently characterized. This study investigated longitudinal changes in electrocardiographic markers of ventricular repolarization following anti-TNF therapy in patients with RA. Methods: This retrospective longitudinal study included 115 patients with RA who initiated anti-TNF therapy and had clinical, laboratory, and 12-lead electrocardiographic assessments at baseline and after approximately 24 weeks. Ventricular repolarization was evaluated using QT, corrected QT (QTc), Tpeak-Tend (Tp-e), corrected Tp-e (cTp-e), and Tp-e/QT. Cross-sectional associations between repolarization indices and inflammatory/disease-related variables were assessed at 24 weeks, together with longitudinal correlations between changes in these variables and changes in repolarization indices. Results: The mean age was 54.4 ± 12.2 years, and 81.7% of participants were women. After 24 weeks of treatment, significant reductions were observed in CRP, ESR, DAS28-CRP, and HAQ scores (all p < 0.001). The Tp-e interval decreased from 85.1 ± 13.6 to 75.3 ± 13.5 ms, and the Tp-e/QT ratio decreased from 0.20 ± 0.04 to 0.18 ± 0.03 (both p < 0.001), with moderate within-subject effect sizes for both changes (Cohen's dz = 0.46). At 24 weeks, Tp-e and Tp-e/QT were positively correlated with inflammatory markers, disease activity, functional impairment, and disease duration. However, longitudinal change-to-change analyses showed no consistent associations between changes in inflammatory/disease activity measures and changes in repolarization indices, except for a weak correlation between ΔDAS28-CRP and ΔTp-e ( r = 0.201, p = 0.031). Despite a significant reduction in mean QTc, the proportion of patients with prolonged QTc remained unchanged (18.3% at both assessments; McNemar p = 1.00). Conclusions: Anti-TNF therapy in patients with RA was associated with significant improvements in several ECG-derived ventricular repolarization indices alongside reductions in inflammatory and disease activity. However, the lack of consistent longitudinal correlations and the unchanged prevalence of prolonged QTc indicate that these findings should be interpreted as treatment-associated changes rather than evidence of a direct electrophysiological or antiarrhythmic effect of TNF inhibition. Prospective controlled studies incorporating clinical cardiovascular outcomes are warranted.

items.title: Complete Blood Count-Derived Inflammatory Indices Following Whole-Body Cryotherapy Combined with Kinesiotherapy Versus Kinesiotherapy Alone in Men with Ankylosing Spondylitis.
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: The response of complete blood count (CBC)-derived inflammatory indices to whole-body cryotherapy (WBC) in ankylosing spondylitis (AS) remains unknown. This exploratory post hoc secondary analysis examined whether adding WBC to kinesiotherapy was associated with differences in these indices and explored their associations with disease activity, pain, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP) levels. Prospectively collected data from 32 men with AS were analyzed. Participants were allocated by alternation, rather than randomization, to WBC combined with kinesiotherapy (WBC + K; n = 16) or kinesiotherapy alone (KT; n = 16). Methods: Prospectively collected data from 32 men with ankylosing spondylitis (AS) who participated in a prior study were analyzed. Participants were allocated to whole-body cryotherapy combined with kinesiotherapy (WBC + K; n = 16) or kinesiotherapy alone (KT; n = 16). Complete blood count parameters, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP) levels, Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Index (BASDAI), and visual analogue scale (VAS) pain scores were assessed prospectively before and after the intervention. Previously unpublished complete blood count data were used to calculate the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), monocyte-to-lymphocyte ratio (MLR), systemic immune-inflammation index (SII), and systemic inflammation response index (SIRI) post hoc and to explore their associations with hsCRP, BASDAI, and VAS pain. The primary intervention effects were assessed using baseline-adjusted analysis of covariance, and the five treatment-effect p -values were subjected to Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Comparisons of changes from baseline were performed as sensitivity analyses. Results: None of the baseline-adjusted between-group treatment effects for NLR, PLR, MLR, SII, or SIRI were statistically significant before or after false discovery rate correction. The adjusted between-group difference for MLR was -0.033 (95% confidence interval: -0.074 to 0.008; p = 0.115; q = 0.329). In the change-score sensitivity analysis, the between-group difference in MLR change was nominally significant ( p = 0.012) but did not meet the multiplicity-adjusted significance threshold ( q = 0.060). Within the WBC + K group, PLR, MLR, and SIRI decreased significantly, whereas no corresponding within-group changes were observed in the KT group; however, these within-group findings were descriptive and did not establish an additional effect of WBC. Changes in the indices were not significantly correlated with changes in hsCRP, BASDAI, or VAS pain. None of the exploratory post-treatment correlations remained significant after multiple-testing correction. Conclusions: This study did not provide baseline-adjusted or multiplicity-adjusted evidence that adding WBC to kinesiotherapy affected any of the investigated CBC-derived inflammatory indices in men with AS. The nominal MLR signal identified in the change-score sensitivity analysis and the within-group reductions in PLR, MLR, and SIRI should be considered exploratory and hypothesis-generating. Larger, prospectively designed, adequately powered randomized studies with prespecified outcomes and baseline-adjusted analyses are required.

items.title: Host-Microbe Crosstalk in Sjögren's Disease: Epithelial Type I Interferon Amplification, Loss of Short-Chain Fatty Acid Restraint, and the Effector-Phase Focus of Validated Therapy.
items.abstract: Sjögren's disease (SjD) is a systemic autoimmune disease of the exocrine glands, long framed as a lymphocyte-driven disorder in which immune cells destroy the target tissue. Genomic, epigenetic, microbiome, and single-cell and spatial studies have since shown the glandular epithelium and the microbial environment to be active participants rather than passive bystanders. This review asks whether host susceptibility and microbiome change can be joined into one continuous axis, following it from genetic and epigenetic susceptibility, through microbiome change read functionally rather than taxonomically, to the crosstalk that converts microbial signals into a host response and the cell states carrying it in human tissue. Two axes run through the whole sequence: the type I interferon (IFN) response and short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) metabolism. Read against them, every disease-modifying therapy with validated efficacy so far acts in the downstream B-cell effector axis, whereas the upstream IFN axis has yielded no established treatment. Because the microbial layer and the salivary gland transcriptome or proteome have never been measured in the same patients, the model proposed here remains a testable hypothesis rather than a completed causal chain. The aim is to specify that model, the falsification conditions it carries, and the study design its verification requires.

items.title: Preclinical Mouse Models of Rheumatoid Arthritis: Comparative Insights into Inflammatory Mediators and Immune Cells.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by persistent synovial inflammation, progressive cartilage destruction, and bone erosion. Mouse models are essential for investigating RA pathogenesis, defining immune-cell and cytokine networks, and evaluating potential therapies. Common models include collagen-induced arthritis (CIA), collagen antibody-induced arthritis (CAIA), human TNF transgenic (hTNF-Tg) arthritis, and SKG arthritis, each representing distinct inflammatory mechanisms. CIA involves adaptive and innate immune cells, including CD4 + T cells, B cells, dendritic cells, macrophages, and neutrophils, with prominent roles for TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-17A, GM-CSF, and IL-23. CAIA primarily reflects antibody-mediated and innate immune mechanisms involving neutrophils, macrophages, complement, and Fcγ receptors, with contributions from TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, GM-CSF, CXCL1, and CXCL2. The hTNF-Tg model highlights chronic TNF-driven inflammation involving macrophages and neutrophils and downstream inflammatory mediators such as IL-1β, IL-6, CXCL1, and CCL2. In contrast, the SKG model emphasizes autoreactive CD4 + T-cell and Th17 responses, with IL-17A, IL-6, and IL-23 contributing to arthritis following environmental stimulation. Collectively, these models are mechanistically complementary and provide distinct insights into immune activation, cytokine signaling, and joint pathology. However, differences in immune regulation, disease heterogeneity, and inflammatory mechanisms between mice and humans emphasize the importance of careful model selection and interpretation. This review summarizes major mouse models of RA, focusing on their immune-cell and inflammatory mediator networks, therapeutic applications, and translational relevance to human disease.

items.title: Positivity Rates and Serum Levels of Antibodies Against Histone H3 Lysine 9 and Its Lactylated Form in Rheumatoid Arthritis and Its Mimics.
items.abstract: Background/Objectives : To compare the positivity rates and serum levels of antibodies against histone H3 lysine 9 (anti-H3K9) and its lactylated form (anti-H3K9la) among patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), or Sjögren disease (SjD) and controls. Methods : Serum anti-H3K9 and anti-H3K9la levels were measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay from 93 patients with RA, 40 with SLE, 40 with SjD, and 40 controls. Antibody findings were compared across study groups and according to rheumatoid factor immunoglobulin M (RF-IgM) and anti-citrullinated protein antibody (ACPA) status in RA. Results: Anti-H3K9 positivity was 28.0% in RA, 40.0% in SLE, 0% in SjD, and 2.5% in controls. Anti-H3K9la positivity was 22.6% in RA and 20.0% in SLE; no SjD patients or controls were positive. Patients with SjD had lower levels of both antibodies than controls. No statistically significant differences were detected according to RF-IgM or ACPA status, although the seronegative subgroups were small. In exploratory multivariable models, TNF inhibitor use was associated with higher levels of both antibodies. Adding either antibody to ACPA and RF-IgM increased sensitivity at the expense of specificity. Conclusions: Anti-H3K9 and anti-H3K9la antibodies were detected more frequently in RA and SLE than in controls, whereas patients with SjD had lower serum levels of both antibodies. No statistically significant differences in antibody positivity or levels were detected according to RF-IgM or ACPA status in RA, although the small seronegative subgroups limited the precision of these comparisons. Their potential value as adjunctive diagnostic biomarkers requires confirmation in larger, independent cohorts with formal diagnostic-performance analyses.

items.title: Programmed cell death: immune regulatory mechanisms in periodontitis and rheumatoid arthritis.
items.abstract: Periodontitis and rheumatoid arthritis, as chronic inflammatory diseases that share epidemiological associations and immunopathological characteristics, have various forms of programmed cell death (PCD) that play a core role in their pathogenesis, which form an important link between the two. The comorbidity of periodontitis and rheumatoid arthritis suggests that there might be a common immune regulatory mechanism, with PCD pathways playing a key role in regulating immune responses. Particularly, the Th17/Treg imbalance and apoptosis resistance in CD4 + CD28 - T cells emerge as shared T cell-centered mechanisms bridging periodontal infection to rheumatoid autoimmunity. Studying how PCD works in periodontitis and rheumatoid arthritis can help uncover the potential links between the two diseases, which provides new targets for clinical treatment and improves patient prognosis. In this article, we'll review relevant research and discuss how PCD is important for immune regulation in periodontitis and rheumatoid arthritis, which provides a theoretical basis for future treatment strategies for both conditions, helping to control the progression of inflammation more effectively.

items.title: Serum SPP1 levels are associated with disease severity and 1-year mortality in primary Sjögren's syndrome-associated interstitial lung disease.
items.abstract: Clinical significance of serum secreted phosphoprotein 1 (SPP1) in primary Sjögren's syndrome-associated interstitial lung disease (pSS-ILD) remains unclear. In this study, we analyzed the GSE47460 lung tissue expression profile to validate SPP1 upregulation in ILD and performed GSEA to explore the potential mechanisms. A retrospective clinical cohort of 88 pSS-ILD patients and 40 healthy controls (HC) was established, with patients stratified into stable disease (SD, n=60) and acute exacerbation (AE, n=28). Serum SPP1 levels were measured by ELISA, and correlations with pulmonary function were analyzed. ROC curves, Kaplan-Meier survival analysis, and Cox regression models were used to evaluate its predictive value. SPP1 was upregulated in ILD lung tissues, with GSEA revealing enrichment of nucleotide metabolism in the high-expression group. Serum SPP1 levels were significantly elevated in pSS-ILD patients compared to HCs [37.69 (27.25-73.42) vs. 20.11 (15.68-23.72) ng/mL, P<0.001], and further increased in the AE group [85.90 (48.67-122.45) vs. 31.45 (25.87-42.02) ng/mL, P<0.001]. SPP1 levels correlated negatively with DLCO% predicted (r = -0.426, P<0.01, q = 0.013). The AUC for distinguishing AE was 0.891, and for predicting 1-year mortality was 0.712. Using a cut-off of 40.41 ng/mL, higher SPP1 levels were associated with worse survival (P = 0.002), and multivariate Cox regression identified SPP1 as an independent risk factor for 1-year mortality (HR = 1.016, 95% CI: 1.006-1.025, P = 0.001). Collectively, these clinical findings demonstrate that serum SPP1 levels correlate with disease severity and may serve as a predictor of poor prognosis in pSS-ILD.

items.title: Frequency and factors associated with flare-ups in lupus patients with lupus nephritis in French Guiana.
items.abstract: French Guiana ranks among the French overseas territories with the highest prevalence of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). However, local data on lupus flares and renal involvement remain limited. This study aimed to determine the frequency of lupus flares and identify associated factors among patients with lupus nephritis (LN) compared with those without renal involvement. We conducted an observational historical cohort study using data from the West Guyanese lupus cohort between January 2018 and December 2022. Patients with confirmed SLE were consecutively included and classified according to the presence or absence of LN. Clinical, biological, and immunological data were extracted from medical records. Lupus flare was defined as documented disease worsening requiring therapeutic intensification. Factors associated with flares were assessed using multivariable logistic regression. Sixty-two patients were included, of whom 45 (72.6%) had LN. Overall, 53% experienced at least one flare. Flares occurred more frequently in patients with LN than in those without LN (62.2% vs. 29.4%). Higher anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith antibody levels, higher SLEDAI scores, fever, pleural effusion, and cutaneous manifestations were significantly associated with flares. In multivariable analysis, LN (OR 3.64; 95% CI 1.00-13.23; p=0.049) and higher anti-dsDNA antibody levels (p=0.033) were independently associated with flares. Lupus flares were frequent and occurred more often in patients with LN. LN and higher anti-dsDNA antibody levels were independently associated with flares, supporting close monitoring of patients with renal involvement to identify disease activity and optimize management.

items.title: Machine learning-based identification of CXCL13 and CXCL10 as key biomarkers in rheumatoid arthritis.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is one of the autoimmune diseases that involve joint damage and synovial membrane inflammation. There have been many attempts to examine the utility of biomarkers in the diagnosis of RA, but there is no clinically accepted biomarker for the diagnosis of RA due to its heterogeneity. Thus, in this study, we tried to find RA biomarkers using machine learning and bioinformatics approaches. Three corresponding gene expression datasets (GSE55457, GSE12021, and GSE77298) were downloaded from the Gene Expression Omnibus database. Batch effect correction was carried out using the ComBat function of the sva package in R. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) compared to controls were identified using limma . To identify the biological functions and pathways of DEGs, Gene Ontology, KEGG, and gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) were conducted. The protein-protein interaction (PPI) network was constructed in Cytoscape using the STRING database. Genes identified through PPI analysis and further filtered by LASSO and SVM-RFE regressions were considered as diagnostic biomarkers. Additional analysis of hub genes was conducted using the GSE89408 dataset. CIBERSORTx was used to evaluate the immune cell infiltration in RA. A total of 440 DEGs were selected, including 197 downregulated and 243 upregulated genes. The DEGs were involved in biological processes and pathways associated with the immune system and were suggested by functional enrichment analysis. GSEA enriched in cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction, hematopoietic cell lineage, primary immunodeficiency, and RA pathways. The hub genes CXCL13 and CXCL10 were chosen with the help of a machine learning algorithm. An external independent validation of the hub genes was conducted. In addition, ROC analysis showed a good diagnostic value of the two genes. The analysis of immune cell infiltration showed CXCL13 was associated with multiple immune-cell populations, including plasma cells, T-cell subsets, and M1 macrophages, whereas CXCL10 showed significant associations with M1 macrophages, plasma cells, and selected T-cell subsets. Correlation analysis showed a high correlation between chemokines CXCL13 and CXCL10 and many infiltrated immune cells. The present study indicates the potential usefulness of CXCL13 and CXCL10 genes as diagnostic biomarkers in RA. Synovial inflammation in RA is associated with the coordinated action of many genes involved in the recruitment of various immune cells to the inflammatory site. Although the term chemokines were used to designate them, these genes are the genes encoding molecules associated with the migration of particular immune cell types, and CXCR5 and CXCR3 may be considered the potential targets for future research.

items.title: Integrative population genetics and multi-omics reveal IL15RA as a shared pathogenic hub in rheumatoid arthritis-related heart failure.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) patients face a significantly elevated risk of heart failure (HF), but population-level evidence and underlying mechanisms remain unclear. We aimed to assess the RA-HF association using national data and identify dietary compounds targeting shared inflammatory pathways. We analyzed NHANES data (n=2,931) and performed two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR). Integrated machine learning, single-cell transcriptomics, clinical samples, and in vitro experiments identified therapeutic targets and evaluated the effectiveness of dioscin (a yam-derived saponin). The rate of HF in RA patients is high, and RA patients with HF have a worse prognosis. MR analysis also revealed that RA was a significant HF risk factor. IL15RA emerged as a shared causal target, whose silencing suppressed TNF-α-induced ICAM-1 in endothelial cells and reduced M1 (CD86 + ) macrophage polarization. Mechanistically, MIF signaling were strongly implicated in the crosstalk between endothelial cells and macrophages. Dioscin bound IL15RA and reduced its expression in both cell types, phenocopying IL15RA silencing. This study identifies IL15RA as a key therapeutic target linking RA and HF, and dioscin as a dietary phytochemical with anti-inflammatory potential. Our findings provide a population-based framework and a readily translatable nutritional strategy for mitigating cardiac comorbidity in RA patients.

items.title: T-cell metabolic reprogramming in systemic lupus erythematosus: linking intracellular metabolism to effector differentiation and senescent-like/exhausted-like states.
items.abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by immune dysregulation and multiorgan inflammation. T-cell metabolic reprogramming has recently emerged as an active area of investigation in the pathogenesis of SLE. This metabolic reprogramming, which involves glycolysis, mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, glutamine metabolism, and lipid metabolism, is associated not only with functional alterations in SLE T cells but also with changes in their differentiation and proliferation, potentially contributing to disease pathogenesis and progression. Moreover, metabolic alterations, including mitochondrial dysfunction and reactive oxygen species accumulation, in the context of persistent T-cell activation may contribute to phenotypic transitions toward senescent-like or exhausted-like states. These two partially overlapping but biologically distinct cellular phenotypes may represent divergent cellular responses to chronic inflammatory stimulation. Rather than representing mutually exclusive states or a simple loss of function, both may contribute to the perpetuation of chronic inflammation, immune imbalance and disease activity. This review summarizes recent advances in T-cell metabolic reprogramming in SLE and its potential relationship to senescent-like and exhausted-like T-cell states.

items.title: A comparison of clinical phenotype and outcomes in anti- melanoma differentiation-associated protein 5 dermatomyositis and anti-synthetase syndrome in a multiethnic cohort in Singapore.
items.abstract: This study aimed to compare the clinical characteristics and outcomes of anti-MDA5 dermatomyositis (MDA5-DM) and anti-synthetase syndrome (ASyS) in a multi-ethnic Southeast Asian cohort, and identify features that facilitate phenotypic differentiation and prognostic stratification. Chart review was performed on consecutive idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIM) patients managed at our centre from January 2015 to June 2021. Patients were classified using the 2017 EULAR/ACR IIM criteria, 2017 European Neuromuscular Centre criteria for immune-mediated necrotising myopathy (IMNM), and Connor's criteria for ASyS. Overlap myositis (OM) was defined as IIM in association with an underlying connective tissue disease or in the presence of a myositis-associated autoantibody. Rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease (RP-ILD) was defined as dyspnoea and/or hypoxaemia with worsening radiologic interstitial lung changes within 3 months of respiratory symptoms onset. Among 119 IIM patients, dermatomyositis was the predominant subtype (57.1%), followed by ASyS (23.5%), OM (15.1%), and IMNM (4.2%). Anti-MDA5 antibodies were detected in 35.3% of dermatomyositis. MDA5-DM and ASyS exhibited comparable demographic characteristics. Anti-Jo1 ( n  = 14) was the commonest anti-tRNA synthetase antibody detected amongst ASyS patients. Compared with ASyS, MDA5-DM demonstrated significantly more prominent cutaneous manifestations-cutaneous ulcers, palmar papules, violaceous rash, Gottron's sign, inverse Gottron's sign, periungual erythema, and heliotrope rash (all p  < 0.017); musculoskeletal features were similar between groups. Median peak creatine kinase levels were significantly higher in ASyS than MDA5-DM patients (median [IQR] 1317 [269-2713] vs. 227 [100-518] U/L; Hodges-Lehmann estimate = 773.5 U/L, 95% CI 150-1,788 U/L). ILD occurred in 42.0% of all IIM-subtypes; 78.9% of dermatomyositis-ILD cases were anti-MDA5 positive. RP-ILD was identified in 14 patients, of which 8 cases were anti- MDA5-DM and 4 ASyS. MDA5-DM/ASyS patients with RP-ILD had higher median peak AST levels (median [IQR] 103.5 [88-343] vs. 59 [44-119] U/L; Hodges-Lehmann estimate = 51 U/L, 95% CI 8-191 U/L) and markedly increased mortality compared with those without RP-ILD (75.0% vs. 12.5%; absolute risk difference 62.5%, 95% CI 35.7%-89.3%). The 1-year survival rates were 18.8% (95% CI 1.1%-53.5%) among MDA5-DM patients with RP-ILD, 75.0% (95% CI 12.8%-96.1%) among ASyS patients with RP-ILD and 97.4% (95% CI 83.2%-99.6%) among MDA5-DM or ASyS patients without RP-ILD. Survival differed significantly across these 3 groups (log rank p  < 0.001). In our cohort, MDA5-DM and ASyS shared high burden of ILD but differed in cutaneous manifestations, risk of RP-ILD and survival, highlighting important diagnostic and prognostic distinctions warranting further investigation and informing clinical management.

items.title: Synchronous Physical Telerehabilitation Versus Face-to-Face Rehabilitation in Axial Spondyloarthritis: A Focused Narrative Review.
items.abstract: Background and Objectives : Exercise is central to axSpA management, but whether live remote delivery preserves effects of the same face-to-face program is uncertain. Methods : Five databases were searched until 9 September 2026; registry, reference, and citation searches ended on 11 September 2026. Reports from one trial were linked; contextual studies were illustrative. Results : Of 214 database records, 123 unique records were screened, and 11 reports representing eight studies were selected from the five databases. A ClinicalTrials.gov record and doctoral thesis linked to the Karaca trial were obtained separately and were not counted among those 11 database-selected reports. One assessor-blinded RCT compared the same individualized clinical Pilates program by videoconference or in clinic. Fifty participants were randomized, 46 assessed at eight weeks, and 40 at six months. Median BASFI improvement was 3.0 versus 2.5 points at eight weeks ( p = 0.587) and 2.0 versus 2.0 points at six months ( p = 0.838). Mann-Whitney U tests used α = 0.017; between-group effect estimates and 95% confidence intervals were unavailable. All-randomized attendance was 93.8% versus 94.0%. Five participants reported transient symptoms; three serious events were judged unrelated, and no intervention-related serious adverse event was reported. Conclusions : Remote delivery was implementable with high short-term attendance among digitally eligible participants. This trial does not establish equivalence, non-inferiority, preserved effect, broad accessibility, or a safety profile. Adequately powered non-inferiority trials are needed.

items.title: Detection of Neutrophil Extracellular Traps by Flow Cytometry in Healthy Controls and Patients with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus.
items.abstract: Excessive induction of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) formation (NETosis) and clearance system dysfunction lead to autoantigen accumulation, initiating autoimmune cascades in immune-mediated inflammatory rheumatic diseases. This study aims to quantitatively determine NETs using multicolor flow cytometry to evaluate the pathogenic role of NETosis in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). The study enrolled 70 patients with a verified diagnosis of SLE (median age 38.0 [27.5; 46.0] years; 62 females, 8 males). The control group consisted of 20 sex- and age-matched healthy individuals. Laboratory evaluation included multicolor flow cytometry, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), and indirect immunofluorescence assay. NETosis induction was performed using phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA). The proportion of neutrophils undergoing NETosis following PMA stimulation was significantly higher in SLE patients than in healthy controls (69.3% versus 27.5%, respectively, p = 0.0006). Conversely, serum levels of citrullinated histone H3 (measured by ELISA) were significantly higher in healthy controls compared to SLE patients ( p = 0.005). The systemic immune-inflammation index (SII) was substantially higher in the SLE group compared to the healthy control group (613.9 versus 27.5, p less than 0.05). Furthermore, the percentages of both spontaneous and PMA-induced NETs demonstrated significant differences in patients with severe disease courses. The developed methodological approach based on multiparametric flow cytometry serves as an objective monitoring tool and could be recommended for verifying inflammatory activity in patients with a long-standing history of SLE exceeding 2 years.

items.title: Total Flavonoids of Rhizoma Drynariae Ameliorate Rheumatoid Arthritis by Modulating Macrophage Polarization and HIF-1α-Associated Glycolysis.
items.abstract: Objective: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease with the abnormal accumulation of pro-inflammatory macrophages within the synovial joints. Total flavonoids of Rhizoma Drynariae (TFRD), the major bioactive constituents of the traditional Chinese medical herb Drynariae rhizome , have shown potent activities in treating RA, but their effect and underlying mechanism in modulating macrophage behavior remain unknown. This study aimed to evaluate the therapeutic potential of TFRD in regulating macrophage polarization during RA, and to further elucidate the underlying mechanism. Methods: The therapeutic effects of TFRD were assessed by utilizing a collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) mice model in vivo. A macrophage polarization model was employed to investigate the effect of TFRD on the macrophage pro-inflammatory polarization and glycolytic activity in vitro. Additionally, the role of hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α) in the TFRD-mediated regulation of macrophage glycolysis was examined via plasma transfection. Results: Administration of TFRD significantly reduced the arthritis severity scores and ameliorated joint swelling and bone destruction in CIA mice. The therapeutic efficacy of high-dose TFRD (TFRD-H) was broadly similar to that of MTX in CIA mice. Further, TFRD decreased the proportion of pro-inflammatory macrophages and the expression of HIF-1α within the joints of CIA mice. The in vitro experiments indicated that TFRD inhibited the lipopolysaccharide-induced macrophage pro-inflammatory polarization. Mechanistically, TFRD attenuated glycolytic metabolism and downregulated HIF-1α expression during pro-inflammatory polarization, while HIF-1α overexpression partly reversed these effects. Furthermore, 16S rRNA sequencing analysis revealed the mitigated dysbiosis of the gut microbiota and increased relative abundance of Parabacteroides in CIA mice. Conclusions: These findings indicate that TFRD alleviated RA, which was partly dependent on downregulating pro-inflammatory macrophages and mitigating HIF-1α-associated glycolysis. This study could provide a scientific basis for further research and the clinical use of TFRD.

items.title: Lung Ultrasound in Rheumatoid Arthritis-Associated Interstitial Lung Disease: Association with Radiological Patterns, Lung Function Tests, and Disease Activity-A Single-Center Retrospective Cross-Sectional Study.
items.abstract: Introduction: Interstitial lung disease (ILD) represents one of the most relevant extra-articular manifestations in rheumatoid arthritis (RA), and significantly contributes to morbidity and mortality. High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) is the gold standard for the diagnosis of ILD; however, its use in daily practice is limited. Lung ultrasound (LUS) is a non-invasive, repeatable, and bedside tool for ILD assessment. This study aimed to evaluate the association between quantitative LUS score and HRCT findings in RA patients. Methods: We conducted a single-center, retrospective cross-sectional study in RA patients with and without ILD. Demographic, clinical, lung function, and disease activity (DAS28-CRP) data were collected, together with LUS and HRCT findings at baseline. Correlation and regression analyses were performed to evaluate associations between LUS score, HRCT patterns, pulmonary function, and disease activity. Results: Thirty-seven RA subjects (M/F: 20/17; mean age 68.8 ± 10.4 years) were included; ILD was present in 24 patients (64.8%), including 17 (45.9%) with a UIP pattern. LUS score inversely correlated with DLCO (r = -0.413; p = 0.01) and positively with age (r = 0.47; p = 0.003) and DAS28-CRP (r = 0.366; p = 0.02). Higher LUS score were significantly associated with UIP pattern at both uni- (OR 1.09; 95%CI 1.02-1.16; p < 0.01) and multivariable regression analysis adjusted for age (OR 1.07; 95%CI 1.01-1.15; p = 0.02). Likewise, DAS28-CRP was significantly associated with a UIP pattern on chest HRCT in both univariable (OR 3.05, 95% CI 1.30-7.14; p = 0.01) and multivariable analyses adjusted for age (OR 2.35, 95% CI 1.19-6.86; p = 0.02). Conclusions: Overall, higher LUS score values were associated with reduced pulmonary function, higher DAS28-CRP, and the presence of a UIP pattern on chest HRCT. However, these findings should be considered exploratory and require further confirmation in larger prospective studies.

items.title: Transcriptomic Profiling of Oxidative Stress-Associated Immune and Apoptotic Signatures and In Silico Prediction of Therapeutic Candidates for Sjögren's Syndrome Dry Eye.
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Sjögren's syndrome (SS) is a systemic autoimmune disease characterized by lacrimal and salivary gland dysfunction, leading to dry eye and dry mouth. This study aimed to explore the potential associations between oxidative stress-mediated immune and apoptotic responses in Sjögren's syndrome dry eye (SSDE) and to computationally predict theoretical interacting candidates. Methods: We enrolled 16 SSDE patients and 15 healthy controls to assess key clinical parameters. The study utilized conjunctival impression cytology, RNA-seq, and bioinformatics to identify exploratory transcriptomic signatures. Gene expression levels were then assessed using real-time quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR). To provide supportive cross-species biological context regarding local oxidative stress status in vivo, malondialdehyde (MDA) levels were quantified in the extraorbital lacrimal glands of an SSDE murine model (NOD mice vs. BALB/c controls, n = 6/group). Furthermore, molecular docking and 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations were conducted to computationally explore potential pharmacological interventions. Results: Exploratory global transcriptomic analysis indicated that differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were prominently enriched in immune responses, inflammatory signaling, and apoptotic pathways, aiding the identification of a candidate transcriptomic signature of oxidative stress-related DEGs. Preliminary immune infiltration profiling suggested that the abundance levels of CD4+ T cells and eosinophils were positively correlated, while M1 and M2 macrophages were negatively correlated. Exploratory ROC analysis suggested the potential discriminative value (AUC 0.7-0.9) for key disease-associated genes, notably CDKN1A and BAX (r = 0.883). RT-qPCR results demonstrated that the transcription levels of CDKN1A , BAX , TGFBR1 , and S100A9 were significantly higher in the SSDE group compared to the healthy control group ( p < 0.05). Importantly, in vivo biochemical assays provided supportive cross-species evidence of lipid peroxidation, demonstrating a significant elevation in MDA levels in the lacrimal glands of NOD mice compared to controls ( p < 0.01). Furthermore, in silico molecular simulations suggested that natural antioxidants, such as ursolic acid and andrographolide, exhibited favorable predicted binding conformations within the active pockets of CDKN1A and BAX. Conclusions: Supported by exploratory transcriptomic profiling and supportive in vivo biochemical data, our findings highlight an exploratory molecular association between oxidative stress and an intimately coupled immune-apoptotic axis in SSDE pathogenesis. The computational structural evaluation of ursolic acid and andrographolide provides a hypothesis-generating foundation for future in vitro and in vivo pharmacological investigations.

items.title: The Role of Lymphatic System Dysfunction, IL-33, and Neutrophil Extracellular Traps in Rheumatoid Arthritis: A Comprehensive Review.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is sustained not only by immune activation within the synovium but also by dysfunction of the lymphatic network that normally clears interstitial fluid, inflammatory mediators, and leukocytes migrating from inflamed tissues. Functional abnormalities in lymph node stromal cells may arise before clinically apparent arthritis. After RA becomes established, the lymphatic response may shift from compensatory lymphangiogenesis to reduced collecting-vessel contraction, structural deterioration of draining lymph nodes, and impaired lymphatic drainage. This review examines how IL-33/ST2 signaling, neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), and the lymphatic endothelial program maintained by PROX1 may influence the shift from compensatory remodeling to lymphatic dysfunction. During early inflammation, IL-33 can activate the ST2/TRAF6/PI3K/Akt/eNOS/NO pathway in lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs), while VEGF-C/VEGFR3 signaling supports lymphatic vessel growth and fluid transport. But vessel expansion does not guarantee that newly formed lymphatics mature or restore effective drainage. As inflammation persists, TNF-driven iNOS activity, occupation of lymphatic sinuses by B cells, and structural changes in draining lymph nodes can reduce lymphatic transport and prolong synovial exposure to cytokines, immune complexes, and autoantigens. NETs directly injure lymphatic endothelium in inflammatory models outside RA, but direct evidence in synovial LECs remains unavailable. NET-associated histones, proteases, myeloperoxidase, extracellular DNA, and HMGB1 should therefore be considered plausible rather than established mediators of LEC injury through junctional disruption, oxidative stress, or RAGE- and TLR9-related signaling. Reduced PROX1 activity may further weaken lymphatic endothelial identity by disrupting the expression of VEGFR3, LYVE1, PDPN, and CCL21, which support vessel maintenance and immune-cell transport. Based on these findings, we propose a stage-dependent model in which established IL-33-NET-fibroblast-like synoviocyte and IL-33-macrophage circuits increase the inflammatory burden, while declining lymphatic clearance retains the mediators that sustain these circuits. This framework separates demonstrated mechanisms from untested links and identifies synovial LEC injury, lymphatic transport, and stage-specific pathway modulation as priorities for mechanistic studies and therapeutic development.

items.title: Deciphering the Therapeutic Effect of Quercetin-Loaded Pumpkin Seed Oil Nanoemulsion on Rheumatoid Arthritis in a Rat Model.
items.abstract: Background: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic systemic autoimmune disorder characterized by persistent synovitis, progressive joint destruction, and significant morbidity. Despite advances in targeted therapies, achieving sustained remission remains challenging, necessitating the exploration of novel, multi-targeted therapeutic strategies. This study investigates the therapeutic potential of a self-emulsifying nanoformulation, quercetin-loaded pumpkin seed oil nanoemulsion (Qu-PSONE), in a complete Freund's adjuvant (CFA)-induced RA rat model, focusing on elucidating its integrated molecular mechanisms. Methods: Adult male Wistar rats (n = 50) were divided into a normal control group (n = 10) and an RA-induced rat model (n = 40), with the latter being further subdivided into four experimental groups: RA control, free quercetin (Qu), pumpkin seed oil nanoemulsion (PSONE), and Qu-PSONE-treated groups. We performed comprehensive analyses, including physicochemical characterization of the nanoformulations and quantification of synovial protein levels of key mediators (IL-17, TLR-4, NF-κBp65, Nrf2, OPG, RANKL, JAK1, and STAT3) via ELISA. In parallel, synovial gene expression of GSDMD and miRNA-146a was assessed using RT-qPCR. Treatment efficacy was further evaluated through paw thickness measurements, clinical arthritis scoring, radiographic assessment of joint erosion, and histopathological examination, alongside immunohistochemical staining for TNF-α and MMP-9. Results: Our findings demonstrate that Qu-PSONE exerts a superior nutrigenomic inhibitory effect on the inflammatory cascade and joint deformity associated with CFA-induced adjuvant arthritis. The Qu-PSONE significantly modulated miRNA-146a expression, serving as a sensitive indicator of attenuated synoviocyte activation. This treatment concurrently increased Nrf2 synovial level, suppressed synovial NF-κBp65, TLR-4, and IL-17 levels, which in turn downstream-inhibited the JAK/STAT pathway, balanced RANKL/OPG signaling, and downregulated transcriptional priming of the pyroptotic marker GSDMD . Together, these findings demonstrate that Qu-PSONE effectively breaks the inflammatory cascade in adjuvant arthritis. These palliative effects of Qu-PSONE were robustly correlated with reduced paw edema, improved arthritis scores, mitigated radiographic joint damage, and diminished synovial infiltration and MMP-9 expression, as confirmed by histological and immunohistochemical analyses. Conclusions: Qu-PSONE halts arthritic progression and curtails joint damage through multitarget suppression of the NF-κBp65/TLR-4/IL-17 inflammatory axis at the synovial level. This response is accompanied by reduced JAK1 and STAT3 protein expression, re-established RANKL/OPG homeostasis to mitigate bone destruction, and attenuated GSDMD transcript levels, with miRNA-146a serving as a responsive biomarker of disease resolution.

items.title: Patterns of Mutual Associations Within the IL-12 Cytokine Family in Systemic Sclerosis Patients: A Pilot Study.
items.abstract: Objectives: This study aimed to investigate the associations among cytokines of the IL-12 family in patients with systemic sclerosis (SSc) and to evaluate their relationships with the pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-α and IL-6, the latent form of TGF-β1 (LAP-bound, without prior sample activation), clinical parameters, and disease subtypes. Methods: Concentrations of IL-12p70, IL-12p40, IL-23, IL-27, IL-35, IL-39, TNF-α, and IL-6 were measured in serum, whereas latent TGF-β1 concentrations were determined in plasma obtained from 60 patients with systemic sclerosis (SSc) and 21 age- and sex-matched healthy controls. Results: Compared with healthy controls, patients with SSc exhibited significantly elevated levels of IL-12p40, IL-23, and IL-35, whereas IL-27, TNF-α, and TGF-β concentrations were significantly reduced. Correlation analysis revealed significant negative associations between latent TGF-β1 and IL-6, IL-27, and IL-35. Significant positive correlations were observed between TNF-α and IL-6, TNF-α and IL-12p40, IL-35 and IL-12p40, IL-23 and IL-12p40, and IL-12p40 with both IL-6 and IL-12p70. No significant associations were identified between the investigated cytokines and the Medsger severity score, patient age, anti-centromere antibody (ACA) status, anti-topoisomerase I antibody (Scl-70) status, the presence of pulmonary fibrosis, or diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide (DLCO). In contrast, IL-35 levels demonstrated significant moderate negative correlations with both the modified Rodnan Skin Score (mRSS) (ρ = -0.35, p < 0.01) and disease duration (ρ = -0.30, p < 0.05). Conclusions: These findings may indicate the presence of a complex network of associations among IL-12 family cytokines in systemic sclerosis.

items.title: BDNF Val66Met (rs6265) in Ankylosing Spondylitis: A Descriptive Genotype-Phenotype Study in a Romanian Cohort.
items.abstract: Background: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a chronic inflammatory disease with musculoskeletal and extra-articular manifestations and associated cardiometabolic comorbidity. Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) is involved in pain processing, neuroplasticity, inflammatory signaling, and metabolic regulation. The functional BDNF Val66Met polymorphism (rs6265) affects intracellular trafficking and activity-dependent BDNF secretion, but its clinical relevance in AS remains poorly characterized. This study evaluated the distribution of BDNF Val66Met and explored its associations with disease activity, inflammation, pain, depressive symptoms, and metabolic parameters in patients with AS. Methods: This single-center, cross-sectional study included 81 patients with AS and no healthy control group. Genotyping was performed using a tetra-primer amplification refractory mutation system polymerase chain reaction (T-ARMS-PCR) assay. Clinical assessment included the Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Index (BASDAI), Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Score based on C-reactive protein (ASDAS-CRP), pain Numerical Rating Scale (NRS), and depression subscale of the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS-D), together with CRP and metabolic measurements. ASDAS-CRP was designated as the primary clinical outcome. Statistical analyses included the Mann-Whitney U test, Fisher's exact test, Spearman correlation with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction, Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium testing, and exploratory multivariable linear and logistic regression. Results: The cohort comprised 81 patients (61 men and 20 women; mean age 53.2 ± 12.5 years). T-ARMS-PCR yielded 57 GG (70.4%) and 24 GA (29.6%) genotype calls, with no AA banding pattern observed; the Met allele frequency was 14.8%. The genotype calls were not independently confirmed by sequencing or restriction fragment length polymorphism analysis. No significant associations were identified between genotype and the clinical, inflammatory, or metabolic variables. Genotype was not associated with ASDAS-CRP after adjustment for age, sex, disease duration, current biologic-therapy status, and current smoking status (B = 0.045, 95% CI -0.238 to 0.328, p = 0.754; n = 80). After Benjamini-Hochberg correction, pain NRS remained correlated with BASDAI and CRP, while HADS-D remained correlated with BASDAI. Metabolic syndrome was present in 24 of 81 participants (29.6%) according to the harmonized Joint Interim Statement definition; medication use for individual metabolic components was not systematically available. Conclusions: No evidence of an association between BDNF Val66Met and disease activity, inflammatory markers, depressive symptoms, or metabolic parameters was found in this AS cohort. This study had 80% power to only detect an effect of Cohen's d ≥ 0.69, and smaller genotype-associated differences cannot be excluded. The findings also describe the cardiometabolic profile of the cohort and the relationships among pain, inflammation, and depressive symptoms.

items.title: Epidemiology of Diabetes Mellitus in Patients With Psoriatic Arthritis: Current Evidence.
items.abstract: Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a common comorbidity of psoriatic arthritis (PsA); however, its global prevalence and the impact of treatment exposure remain unclear. This study aimed to assess the global prevalence of DM in patients with PsA using different subgroup analyses. A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library and the Web of Science was performed from inception until February 2025 for observational studies reporting the prevalence or incidence of DM in PsA patients. Random-effects models were applied to pool estimates, and subgroup, meta-regression, and sensitivity analyses were conducted to explore heterogeneity. Publication bias was evaluated using the Egger's test and the trim-and-fill method. Sixty-three studies, including 293,582 patients with PsA, were analysed. Patients with PsA included in this study were divided into treatment-disclosed and non-treatment-disclosed groups. DM overall prevalence in patients with PsA was 13.84% in the non-treatment-disclosed population and 13.50% in the treatment-disclosed cohort. Geographically, the comorbidity prevalence rates were higher in South America (37.98%) and Asia (16.76%) than in Europe (12.81%) and North America (12.38%) in the non-treatment-disclosed population. In the treatment-disclosed population, prevalence was also highest in South America (28.13%), followed by Asia (18.30%). Meta-regression analysis identified age, type of DM, region, and study design as contributors to heterogeneity. Evidence of small-study effects was detected in the T2DM subgroup and cohorts receiving systemic therapy plus biologics. Subgroup analysis shows that the prevalence of DM is associated with the type of study and the region in which the patients were located. These findings support routine metabolic screening for PsA and highlight the need for longitudinal studies to track disease activity, treatment patterns, and metabolic outcomes.

items.title: Polysaccharide-Derived Drug Delivery Systems: Therapeutic Potential in Rheumatoid Arthritis-A Review.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a systemic autoimmune disease characterized by chronic synovial inflammation, synovial hyperplasia, and progressive joint destruction and remains a major clinical challenge. Polysaccharide-derived delivery platforms have attracted widespread attention for RA precision therapy owing to their natural origin, excellent biocompatibility, and tailorable functionality; however, existing reviews generally focus on single material or carrier types and provide limited cross-comparison of carrier architectures and translational considerations. This review systematically evaluates recent advances in polysaccharide derivative design strategies and delivery system innovations for RA management. We first elaborate on how chemical modifications confer multi-responsive properties (pH-, reactive oxygen species [ROS]-, and enzyme-triggered release) and how diversified morphologies (hydrogels, microspheres, microneedles, vesicles) enable spatiotemporally controlled drug delivery in inflamed joints. Critical analysis highlights several translational barriers, including limited in vivo retention, insufficient pharmacokinetic and biodistribution data, and challenges associated with scale-up manufacturing and reproducibility. Looking forward, future development should integrate biomimetic design, rational multi-component optimization, and advanced manufacturing technologies to improve the stability, controllability, and translational feasibility of polysaccharide-based RA delivery systems. This review provides an integrated, translation-focused perspective that bridges material engineering and clinical pathological demands, guiding the development of next-generation polysaccharide-based RA therapies.

items.title: A Pilot Study on the Ocular Effects of Colchicine in Children with Familial Mediterranean Fever.
items.abstract: Background and Objectives: Myopia is a worldwide healthcare problem, particularly in the young population. Inflammation, alongside genetic and environmental factors, may contribute to the onset and progression of myopia. This pilot study explored whether long-term colchicine therapy is associated with ocular biometric and refractive differences in pediatric patients with Familial Mediterranean Fever (FMF). Materials and Methods: In this cross-sectional study, ocular biometric and refractive parameters were compared between FMF patients receiving colchicine for at least one year and age-matched healthy controls, including refraction, keratometry, anterior chamber depth (ACD), axial length (AL), and ganglion cell complex (GCC). Results: Compared with controls, the colchicine group showed a smaller refractive error (-0.46 ± 1.06 vs. -1.48 ± 1.93 D) and shallower ACD (3.29 ± 0.35 vs. 3.73 ± 0.31 mm); both remained significant after Holm-Bonferroni correction (corrected p = 0.041 and p < 0.001). Keratometry was also lower in the colchicine group but did not remain significant after correction (corrected p = 0.194). AL and GCC did not differ significantly between groups. Conclusions: Colchicine-treated FMF patients showed a less myopic profile and shallower anterior chamber depth than controls. Given the cross-sectional design and the inseparability of FMF status from colchicine treatment, these findings should be considered preliminary and hypothetical rather than evidence of a plausible protective effect, highlighting the need for longitudinal studies to clarify this potential association.

items.title: Biomarkers in ANCA-Associated Vasculitis-Associated Interstitial Lung Disease: A Scoping Review.
items.abstract: Background: Interstitial lung disease (ILD) is an increasingly recognized manifestation of ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV) and is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. The marked biological and clinical heterogeneity of AAV-associated ILD (AAV-ILD) poses major challenges for diagnosis, prognostic stratification, and therapeutic decision-making. Circulating biomarkers have emerged as promising tools for improving disease characterization; however, the available evidence remains limited and fragmented. Methods: We performed a scoping review to summarize the current evidence on circulating biomarkers investigated in AAV-ILD. Peer-reviewed studies evaluating biomarkers associated with ILD occurrence, disease activity, radiological progression, pulmonary function decline, mortality, or treatment response were systematically identified and qualitatively analyzed. Results: Seven observational studies met the inclusion criteria. The identified biomarkers could be broadly classified into three biological categories: epithelial injury biomarkers (KL-6 and SP-D), immune-fibrotic biomarkers (CCL2, CXCL6, CXCL13, and IL-13), and epithelial remodelling biomarkers (CA19-9, CA125, and CYFRA21-1). KL-6 and SP-D were associated across individual studies with pulmonary involvement, disease activity, or relapse, whereas CCL2, CXCL6, CXCL13, and IL-13 were associated with inflammatory and profibrotic processes, radiological abnormalities, or disease progression. Tumour-associated biomarkers were associated with radiological abnormalities and mortality, suggesting that they may reflect aberrant epithelial remodelling rather than malignancy. Across studies, circulating biomarkers showed preliminary associations with disease detection, prognosis, longitudinal disease behaviour, and treatment response; however, their clinical utility has not been prospectively established. Overall, the current evidence is limited by small sample sizes, retrospective study designs, and substantial clinical heterogeneity. Conclusions: Circulating biomarkers represent a promising approach for improving the biological characterization of AAV-ILD and may contribute to the future characterization of inflammatory and fibrotic disease phenotypes. Prospective multicentre studies with independent validation cohorts are required before biomarker-guided management can be implemented in routine clinical practice.

items.title: Evidence-informed exercise dose targets for rheumatoid arthritis: A systematic review and bayesian dose-response network meta-analysis.
items.abstract: Exercise is strongly recommended as part of integrative management for rheumatoid arthritis (RA). However, most trials and conventional network meta-analyses compare broad exercise categories without explicitly modelling dose, which may obscure non-linear dose-response patterns and limit outcome-specific interpretation. To estimate statistically supported dose ranges and the model-estimated doses associated with the most favourable posterior effects of different exercise modalities on disease activity, pain, physical function, and cardiorespiratory fitness in adults with RA. Eight databases were searched from inception to 16 June 2026 for randomised controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating structured exercise interventions lasting at least 2 weeks in adults with RA. Weekly exercise exposure was standardised as metabolic equivalent minutes per week (MET-min/week) using the 2024 Adult Compendium and treated as a pragmatic proxy of exercise volume across five modalities: aerobic exercise (AE), resistance exercise (RE), combined aerobic and resistance exercise (AE+RE), traditional Chinese exercise (TCE), and yoga. Dose-response relationships for DAS28, VAS pain, HAQ-DI, and VO₂max were estimated using the MBNMAdose package with a quadratic function. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2, and confidence in the evidence was evaluated using CINeMA. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261418955). Forty-four RCTs comprising 93 arms and 3132 participants were included. The fitted dose-response relationships were frequently non-linear or plateauing, and statistically supported effects varied by modality and outcome. TCE produced the largest reduction in DAS28 at 500 MET-min/week (MD -0.84, 95% CrI -1.16 to -0.50). RE produced the largest reductions in VAS pain at 820 MET-min/week (MD -14.03 mm, 95% CrI -19.98 to -8.68) and HAQ-DI at 1000 MET-min/week (MD -0.26, 95% CrI -0.47 to -0.06), whereas AE produced the largest improvement in VO₂max at 750 MET-min/week (MD 4.75 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹, 95% CrI 3.39 to 6.11). Sensitivity analyses suggested that VO₂max findings were the most robust, whereas DAS28 estimates were more sensitive to exclusion of studies at high risk of bias. Meta-regression did not identify clear moderation by age or intervention duration. Confidence in the evidence ranged from very low to moderate across outcomes and comparisons. Exercise management in RA may benefit from an outcome-specific and dose-informed approach rather than a uniform weekly target. Larger model-estimated exercise doses were not consistently associated with greater benefit. Given the very-low-to-moderate confidence in the evidence and inconsistent reporting of adverse events, the estimated dose values should be interpreted as provisional model-based reference targets rather than definitive prescriptions or safety thresholds.

items.title: Structural Alterations of the Temporomandibular Joint in Rheumatoid Arthritis: A Cone-Beam Computed Tomography Study.
items.abstract: Background and Objectives : Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) may involve the temporomandibular joint (TMJ), but structural features distinguishing RA-related involvement from non-RA temporomandibular disorders (TMDs) remain incompletely defined. This study compared quantitative and qualitative cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) findings between patients with RA and a symptomatic non-RA TMD comparison group and explored bilateral asymmetry and associations with RA-related characteristics. Materials and Methods : This single-center retrospective cross-sectional study included 84 adults (42 RA and 42 non-RA TMD). All participants had TMJ-related symptoms or signs and clinically indicated CBCT examinations available. Bilateral CBCT assessment included condylar and mandibular fossa morphometry, joint-space measurements, condylar position, and qualitative osseous abnormalities. Linear mixed-effects models and generalized estimating equations accounted for bilateral observations, with Holm correction for multiple testing. Exploratory clinical associations and intraobserver reliability were also evaluated. Results : Clinical TMJ manifestations did not differ significantly between groups. The inferential analyses showed lower condylar height and anterior joint space and greater condylar length, anteroposterior condylar length, and condylar-to-midsagittal distance in RA. The largest quantitative difference involved condylar height (-5.43 mm; adjusted p < 0.001). Cortical erosions (OR = 5.94; 95% CI, 2.57-13.70) and joint-space narrowing (OR = 3.96; 95% CI, 1.66-9.42) were more strongly associated with RA. Absolute bilateral asymmetry did not differ after multiplicity correction, although group-by-side interactions persisted for condylar height and condylar position. Longer disease duration correlated with greater condylar-height asymmetry (ρ = 0.62; adjusted p < 0.001). Intraobserver reliability was high to excellent. Conclusions : RA-related TMJ involvement appears to reflect combined condylar remodeling, vertical structural loss, altered condyle-fossa relationships, and erosive change rather than uniform degeneration. These findings support CBCT as a potentially useful tool for structural characterization, but prospective multimodal validation using observed patient-level data is required.

items.title: A Preliminary Exploratory Study Based on LC-MS/MS and LFQ for Candidate Protein Biomarkers in Peripheral Blood from Rheumatoid Arthritis.
items.abstract: Objective: Detangling the rheumatoid arthritis (RA) proteomic profile is of interest to improve diagnosis, RA subclassifications, and targeted treatment. We aimed at identifying serum proteins as candidate biomarkers for RA. Methods: This case-control study included participants with RA and healthy controls (HCs) paired by gender; clinical information and proteomic profiles were analyzed for the identification of candidate protein biomarkers. A statistical analysis included logistic regression and ROC curves for AUC measurement. Results: Following the screening of 176 patients, 25 RA and 25 HC patients were included in this study. The average age was 51 ± 12 years, and 90% were females. Notably, we identified five serum protein candidate biomarkers with differential expression when comparing RA to HC, consisting of testis-expressed protein 13B ( p = 6.31 × 10 -4 ), keratin type II cytoskeletal 79 ( p = 1.317 × 10 -4 ), 60 kDa heat shock protein ( p = 7.594 × 10 -4 ), pseudo uridylate synthase 7 homolog ( p = 8.332 × 10 -3 ), and SUN domain-containing protein 3 ( p = 1.883 × 10 -7 ). The first four proteins were predominantly observed in patients with RA, while the last was predominantly identified in the HCs. Conclusions: A distinctive serum candidate biomarker profile consistent in five proteins was identified for RA, suggesting a unique stress-related, inflammatory signature. Collectively, the profile exhibits potential, but our findings must be validated in larger cohort studies, preferably in the context of undifferentiated arthritis before a definitive model for diagnosis is established.

items.title: Severe Immune Thrombocytopenia Associated With Newly Diagnosed Rheumatoid Arthritis and Complicated by a Spontaneous Presacral Haematoma: A Case Report.
items.abstract: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is an acquired autoimmune disorder characterised by isolated thrombocytopenia and a variable bleeding phenotype. Patients may be asymptomatic or may present with bleeding ranging from minor skin or mucosal manifestations to uncommon, potentially life-threatening internal haemorrhage. Its occurrence with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is uncommon, and severe disease may require treatment beyond corticosteroids and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG). We report the case of a 64-year-old woman with recently diagnosed seropositive RA who was found to have a platelet count of 0 x 10 9 /L after presenting with a purpuric rash and recurrent epistaxis. Haemoglobin and white cell count were preserved, and investigations did not identify an infectious, malignant, or bone marrow cause. The platelet count remained critically low despite high-dose dexamethasone, two doses of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), and platelet transfusions. Romiplostim was commenced on day 6, producing a progressive platelet response. Cross-sectional imaging undertaken during the admission identified a presacral haematoma with an initially suspected pseudoaneurysm; repeat triple-phase CT showed stability without active bleeding. The patient was discharged on weekly romiplostim, and her platelet count was 197 x 10 9 /L at the 65-day post-discharge follow-up assessment. This case highlights the rare association between RA and ITP, the importance of excluding alternative causes of thrombocytopenia, and the value of early thrombopoietin receptor agonist therapy when first-line rescue treatment is unsuccessful, as well as the rare occurrence of a pre-sacral hematoma with bleeding at an unusual anatomical site as a complication of severe thrombocytopenia.

items.title: Leukocyte-Poor Platelet-Rich Plasma in Foot and Ankle Tendinopathies in Patients With Spondyloarthritis and Rheumatoid Arthritis: A Dual-Center Observational Study.
items.abstract: Foot and ankle involvement is common in inflammatory rheumatic diseases. Plantar fasciitis frequently occurs in spondyloarthritis (SpA) and psoriatic arthritis (PsA), whereas tibialis posterior tendon involvement is relevant in rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Evidence for platelet-rich plasma (PRP) in autoimmune disease remains limited. This study aimed to evaluate leukocyte-poor PRP (LP-PRP) in SpA/PsA-related plantar fasciitis and RA-related PTT tendinopathy and to assess whether disease activity or structural abnormalities influenced treatment response. This dual-center observational study included adults treated with ultrasound-guided LP-PRP. Outcomes included pain (Numeric Rating Scale (NRS)), power Doppler (PWD) activity, effusion, plantar fascia thickness, MRI-detected bone marrow edema (BME), and partial tendon tears. PRP was characterized according to the DEPA classification and administered without exogenous activation. Generalized Estimating Equation models were used to assess changes over time and interactions. Among 101 patients (68 SpA/PsA; 33 RA), LP-PRP was associated with significant clinical and imaging improvements. In plantar fasciitis, fascia thickness decreased from 0.75 to 0.37 cm and pain from NRS 9 to 1, with resolution of PWD activity. Outcomes were similar between SpA and PsA and were not influenced by disease activity or BME. In RA, pain decreased from 8.36 to 0.48, with resolution of effusion, PWD signal, and partial tears. No disease flares occurred. Ultrasound-guided LP-PRP was associated with substantial clinical and imaging improvement in inflammatory rheumatic foot and ankle tendinopathies, without observed disease flares. Controlled studies using standardized PRP characterization are warranted.

items.title: Evaluation of the Impact of Osteoporosis and Rheumatoid Arthritis on the Outcomes of Nonsurgical Endodontic Therapy: A Prospective Cohort Study.
items.abstract: Osteoporosis (OP) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) can potentially disrupt periapical healing following nonsurgical endodontic therapy (NSET) due to changes in bone metabolism and persistent inflammation. We assigned 80 participants to three groups: healthy controls (n = 40), OP (n = 20), and RA (n = 20). All participants received standardized NSET. We assessed periapical healing using digital radiovisiography and cone-beam computed tomography scans at baseline and one, three, and six months, based on measurements of periapical radiolucency and periapical index (PAI) scores. Data were analyzed using Wilcoxon signed-rank and Kruskal-Wallis tests (p < 0.05). There was statistically significant improvement in radiographic healing among all groups during the six-month study period (p < 0.001). PAI scores at baseline were similar among all groups. Healthy participants had significantly more periapical healing compared with OP and RA groups at six months (p < 0.05). Higher mean values of residual radiolucency and PAI scores were noted among the OP and RA groups. OP and RA groups exhibited delayed periapical healing after NSET when compared with healthy controls; however, all groups experienced significant periapical healing following therapy.

items.title: Posterior Neck Pain as the Initial Manifestation of Giant Cell Arteritis: A Diagnostic Challenge.
items.abstract: Giant cell arteritis (GCA) is a granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis that typically affects the temporal arteries, presenting with temporal headache, jaw claudication, or visual symptoms. However, not all cases follow the classical pattern. We report a rare case of a 75-year-old woman who presented solely with isolated occipital headache and posterior neck pain, with no temporal tenderness, jaw claudication, or visual complaints. On examination, both temporal arteries were thickened and pulseless. Vascular imaging revealed non-compressible circumferential wall thickening and severe luminal occlusion involving the bilateral superficial temporal main trunks as well as their frontal and parietal branches. This striking dissociation between clinical symptoms and vascular involvement highlights that GCA can silently involve the temporal arteries while presenting atypically, underscoring the importance of considering GCA even when the only symptom is occipital headache.
